utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Court Deputy, call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is Case Number IT-02-60-T, The Prosecutor versus Vidoje Blagojevic and Dragan Jokic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Good morning, ladies and gentlemen. We were told that the counsel would like to bring some matters to the attention of this Bench. Yes, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. At the conclusion of yesterday Mr. McCloskey informed me that when during the debriefing sessions of Mr. Deronjic who yesterday pled out, he entered a plea of guilty, and obviously until that point in time I would suspect that the Prosecution would not be able to provide us with any material as a result of those debriefings. But it was brought do Mr. McCloskey's attention that during the debriefing on the evening of the 13th of July, 1995, the famous meeting between Deronjic, Beara, and allegedly Mr. Nikolic, which he has indicated, Mr. Deronjic has indicated that Mr. Nikolic was not there. Now, I have not seen the material. This was a representation made to me by Mr. McCloskey who also indicated to me has not seen the material. So I would if it would be possible for Your Honours to get that information, and if it does exist, I don't wish to reopen cross, but perhaps a question from the Bench may be worth asking the witness, who is under oath, as to whether indeed he was there and how can he account for Mr. Deronjic's version who obviously knew in advance what Mr. Nikolic had agreed to in his statement of facts because it has been widely publicised. And I think this is a critical issue. And again, I wish to point out that from the disclosure material that we have provided, it is obviously that a meeting took place between Deronjic and Beara. The disclosure material does reflect that. And it fits into what I believe is the confabulation process of taking part facts and adding fiction to bolster his own importance and perhaps make himself a more pleasing, shall I put it that way, cooperative witness for the Prosecution in exchange for a lenient sentence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: First of all, Mr. Karnavas, we do not know if Mr. Deronjic is going to be a witness in our case. We don't know yet. Secondly, we have not received any information about that debriefing session, let alone the contents of that debriefing session. Maybe we could turn to Mr. McCloskey who could shed some light on this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. When we get a moment, we will get the debriefing material together and provide it to counsel and everyone. That process is -- assembling it is underway. It's a lot of material, and we're trying to identify the material from 1995. What I told Mr. Karnavas yesterday was my recollections of one of the things that he said that may be contradictory somewhat to some of the testimony as my obligation under Rule 68. It was something to the effect that he didn't think he was there, he might have been there, wasn't there. Went around in that kind of tone, and I think Mr. Karnavas is right, we do need to get the material to see precisely what he said. So I was sort of informally meeting my Rule 68 obligation as I recalled one thing. There may be others. And we will get that material - they're working on it now - hopefully by the end of the day. And as I mentioned, if there's something in there obviously that is relevant for cross-examination, we have no objection to bringing Mr. Nikolic back. And we're deciding on whether he's going to be a witness. I think so. I think he's obviously a historical figure that I think the Court should see. I don't have the energy for him right now, but we'll put him on soon, I believe, and we'll make that official and make the filings as is appropriate. But I would lean towards yes at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Well, Mr. Karnavas, we could mention that meeting, but we have to base our questions on the materials at our hands. We could not base any information on the hearsay evidence. We'll see, you know, how it goes. Yes. Is there anything --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sinatra.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, this morning I filed a letter with the Court confidentially providing the proofing notes that the motion for continuance of live testimony was based upon. And I just would ask the Court now that you have that evidence before you, to reconsider the motion to continue the testimony of Mr. Obrenovic. And as you review this document, you'll see that it differs from what the Prosecutor held out yesterday as the evidence toward Mr. Obrenovic. I'd like to the Court please to look at -- I think it's page 4. There's no numbers there. But the page that begins, "Regarding the documents handled handed over to the Office of the Prosecutor on 2 June 2003 by Dragan Obrenovic" it's only a page and a half. And once again, I would ask you to reconsider the decision that you made yesterday, if you would, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Ms. Sinatra, yesterday I believe we said clearly that the reason for us to deny your motion is that your motion did not provide us with sufficient evidence to constitute some prima facie case for us to act otherwise, the other way around. And so we made a decision to continue the proceedings today. But if you have some evidence, if you have a good cause, of course, we'll consider it. But we have made a decision that we'll continue the proceedings under the condition that you have the right to call him back in the future time. Please give us some time for us to study your documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I will. And you are quite correct. You didn't have this evidence before you, so it sheds a new light on the motion. And I appreciate you reviewing this document and withholding a ruling until later on today. I would like to urge the Court to issue a ruling before Mr. Obrenovic takes the stand on this issue simply because we need, I guess, an order from the Court or some vehicle for Mr. Stojanovic to not just have a cursory review of the documents that are in the Office of the Prosecutor. But he needs some time to go through them. We need to ascertain how many documents need to be translated and get that procedure underway as soon as possible. He only had one hour to review hundreds of documents which he chose 70 out of that might be relevant, but that was without reading the documents in total, and we would like to have time to review the evidence that is in the custody of the Prosecutor at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Ms. Sinatra, I think we'll continue the proceedings today, and I give the opportunity to revisit this issue in the future. So I don't think you are in the disadvantaged position. But we have to finish that witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic or Mr. Obrenovic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Obrenovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Then I would ask the Court to stay the proceedings and allow us to file an immediate request for certification for appeal of this decision, and I have the document. I can file it at the next break, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, if you're not satisfied with our decision, of course you may appeal. But I don't think there's sufficient reason to appeal.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Your Honour, our argument, of course, is that just being able to object to the testimony that Mr. Obrenovic is offering has to be an informed and effective representation of Mr. Jokic. And without the documentation which of course at this point could not be translated, to put Mr. Obrenovic on the stand pre-emptively before we have the evidence to review and before we can even investigate the new 19 pages of debriefing that the Prosecutor has just disclosed to us, I think that although we're listening to his testimony, we have to be prepared to object. We don't know whether it's authentic. We don't know whether there's other issues that he's relying upon until we've reviewed the documents. So I understand the Court's rationale; hear him on direct and then we'll deal with it before the cross starts. But I do believe that the fact that you haven't had the evidence, we don't have any translations and we have new pages that need to be investigated affect the ability to object during the direct examination also.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, whether you're going to appeal or not, that is your right. I don't believe that the Trial Chamber has anything to say on that. But I have to say that pending the decisions of the appeal, we'll continue to hear Mr. Obrenovic because we believe that your right is still intact since we give you the opportunity to revisit this issue at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Okay. I understand the Court's ruling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: But I would like for you to reconsider the motion in light of the evidence that's presented to you at another time today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, the proofing notes in question were provided to everyone on Friday, including the Court. I assume that was well known to everyone based on my statements yesterday. So that -- what she has provided is not new. Everyone has had that since Friday. And again, there's no indication in those proofing notes of any conspiracy. But we also will, if they will work with us to identify whatever they want translated, we'll see to it that that material gets translated as soon as possible. But the vast majority of it has already been translated, but we will work with them to get that material translated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your cooperation. Well, another issue is that yesterday Mr. Blagojevic made a request to raise some questions to Mr. Nikolic. We looked into the Rules of Procedure and Evidence as well as the jurisprudence and the practice of this Tribunal. We believe that since the accused has the counsel to defend his interests, there is no need for him to represent himself again, that is, to ask any questions directly to the witness. That will cause very complicated procedural problems. At the same time, we also recognise that this witness is a very important witness detrimental to his case. So this Bench tentatively suggests two ways to deal with this issue: The first one is that Mr. Blagojevic could write down all the questions and pass that piece of paper to his counsel and ask his counsel to read it out word for word, which means that there should be no change of the contents of the question. The second approach is that according to the rules, the accused has the right to make a statement. If Mr. Blagojevic would like to make a statement, he may do so with the understanding that he won't really give up his right of remaining silent. And this statement is not under oath and should not be cross-examined by the Prosecution. Mr. Blagojevic. THE ACCUSED BLAGOJEVIC: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: What do you think of our suggestions? THE ACCUSED BLAGOJEVIC: [Interpretation] Your Honours, to be quite frank, I had expected you to allow me to put several questions of a very practical matter to the witness. Taking into consideration all the circumstances that surround me, essentially not through any basic fault of mine, I was put in this position by others. And it appears that I will have to continue struggling for the truth, which is what I want to do. My position continues to be clear. Mr. Karnavas is not my counsel, and he's not defending me in this case. I have no contact with him. He brought here - I don't want to offend anyone - I brought here a -- he brought here a person who will prepare the material for cross-examination who is not qualified for this. So everything is being devalued and geared to his own personal interests, which I'm unable to identify. But in any event, this is to the detriment and weakening of my position. I don't think that my asking a few practical questions to Mr. Nikolic would not cause any problems. They would be designed simply to clear up the overall situation which cannot, by reading documents or by any statement of mine, be brought to life in the way in which that would be possible if I were to be allowed to put him -- some questions to him. He cannot avoid answering if I were to do that. So I appeal to you, Your Honours. I have a very profound interest in the truth being established. I think that I will testify in these proceedings, but I don't know how. Under these circumstances, I don't see how I can. I do wish to testify. I do wish to convey my understanding of the situation and my role in it in the interest of truth so that you would have that point of view to consider as well for establishing the truth. What I've heard here so far I think is of such a scope that would warrant my participation, that would benefit all, and would throw light on my situation, my position, my commanding and my work in that critical period. That is why I appeal to you to allow me to do this because Mr. Karnavas has betrayed my faith. I never knew him before we met in the Detention Unit. I showed him 1.000 per cent trust and confidence. He has betrayed that, and he's brought me in a situation when I have to decide to trust him or not. I have decided not to trust him, that he's decided to play around with me, and no one can do that. And that trust cannot be restored in the way he thinks he can restore it, by playing around with me. So I appeal to you once again, allow me to put a couple of practical questions to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Blagojevic, I believe that this Bench has travelled X miles to help you help yourself. You have to understand, we asked you to put your question on a piece of paper and ask somebody to read it out. It's a way to give you a chance to ask questions. The difference is it's not asked by yourself but by somebody else. THE ACCUSED BLAGOJEVIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, please, I'm sorry for interrupting you. That was not my intention. Allow me, I have prepared that. There's no problems with that respect. I don't want to make any uncontrolled statements. I want to put my thoughts in order. But I appeal to you for this possibility, I don't wish to tire you out. Let me tell you this, I don't need to ask the witness because I have to tell the truth. I have to address you when I feel that I have to deal with something, when it is very hard for me. I do wish to address this Honourable Court with these words. Now, whether you will ask him these questions, whether he will answer them or not. It's up to you to decide. I don't need to put the questions directly to the witness. I just wish to bring forth something that I feel I have to do without entering into any legal complications because these are things that I do not understand, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Blagojevic, I believe that the rule gave you the right to make a statement at any time you feel proper, and there's still an opportunity for you to be a witness, to testify before this Court. This is a Tribunal. We have the Rules of Procedures. We have to do everything in accordance with those rules and procedures. As for the counsel issue, the Appeals Chamber has made a decision already. No matter we like it or not, we have to comply with it. I think we should put this matter behind. There's no way for us to do at this moment. If you want directly ask some questions to the witness, I have to say that I'm sorry about that. THE ACCUSED BLAGOJEVIC: [Interpretation] I'm afraid I didn't understand you, Your Honour. I just heard that you said that if I want to ask some questions directly to the witness, I'm sorry about that. That is the part I heard in translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. I mean that you could not directly ask questions to the witness. THE ACCUSED BLAGOJEVIC: [Interpretation] I wish to address Your Honours, to address the Court, to present my reactions regarding my position and in the interest of truth, which I wish to be established.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: So you want to make a statement, if I understand you right? THE ACCUSED BLAGOJEVIC: [Interpretation] I don't know, Your Honour, what a statement means. I don't know what that means. I just thought I would convey what I had intended to say in response to the examination-in-chief and the cross-examination of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, of course you may make a statement, but I have to tell you that anything in the statement you are going to make will be used against you in the future. There's a possibility for that. You have to understand that. If you have counsel, the counsel will tell you what is the right of silence and what are the consequences of making a statement. Do you understand that? THE ACCUSED BLAGOJEVIC: [Interpretation] Yes, that is what I said, that I don't understand the implications of a statement. But I wanted to say what I thought was of essential significance for my position, nothing more than that. If I can't ask the witness any questions, I just wanted to ask you to give me the opportunity to tell you what I had in mind. Because this is very important for me. I think that I need to prove my innocence in this Court, and I will do so to the best of my ability and as far as my intellect allows me to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, you may make a statement, Mr. Blagojevic. And you don't have to prove your innocence because you are innocent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Blagojevic, you may make a statement, and we'll call the witness in. I think the witness is also entitled to hear what you are going to say. You may sit down for a moment. THE ACCUSED BLAGOJEVIC: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know. I don't want to complicate this, but is there any way for counsel and the client to consult on this matter? I have no objection. I think your ideas are great. I just -- seems like we're -- that would be ideal, or he could refuse on the record, then we would know what he wished on that score.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I believe that I've explained to Mr. Blagojevic very clear what are the consequences of making a statement; that is, he somehow gave up his right of silence. Anything he says may be used as evidence against him in this case or may be quoted by other cases as evidence. Mr. Blagojevic, do you understand that? THE ACCUSED BLAGOJEVIC: [Interpretation] I do absolutely, Your Honour. I understand fully.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. So could we have the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I'm sorry for the delay this morning, because we had some procedural matters to discuss.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am here to wait.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Blagojevic made a request to make a statement to address to the Bench, to the Judges. And his request is permitted by this Chamber. He will make a statement addressed to us. We would like you to hear this statement, but -- but you have no right to raise any questions and make any comments. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Blagojevic, you may do so. You may sit down. You may sit down, please. You may sit down while making your statement. THE ACCUSED BLAGOJEVIC: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: THE ACCUSED BLAGOJEVIC: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I shall try to adjust these notes in view of the fact that I am addressing you. So I am interested in learning in which form the information was conveyed from the command of the 2nd Light Infantry Brigade regarding the number of able-bodied Muslim men in the Potocari region on the 11th of July 1995. When I say "in what form," I mean was this information in writing or orally conveyed? After that, I'm also interested in hearing when, what time of day, was the witness, that is, Mr. Momir Nikolic, conveyed that information. When did he receive it? My next query is who conveyed this information to the witness from the command of the 2nd Light Infantry Brigade. Rank, name, and position of that person. My next query: Where was that information archived, if it was in written form? So what happened to it after it was received? Also, I would like to know which person was in charge of intelligence and security affairs in the command of the 2nd Light Infantry Battalion on that day, that is, on the 11th of July 1995. Rank, first, and last name. My next query is whether the chief of the intelligence and security organ in the 1st Bratunac Light Infantry Brigade throughout the duration of my being in command of that same brigade, including in July 1995, so whether the chief of the intelligence and security organ knows that he was never on the list of operations duty in the brigade. He was never listed as a duty operations officer. I would also like to know whether the chief of the intelligence and security organ in the 1st Bratunac Light Infantry Brigade knows that throughout the duration of my command of the 1st Bratunac Light Infantry Brigade he had his own duty based on his own plan outside the list of operations duty in the brigade. And when we have these two facts in mind, I would like to know who ordered Mr. Momir Nikolic to be the duty officer on the night between the 12th and 13th July 1995, and when this order was delivered. My next question which I would like the witness who testified in this Honourable Chamber to respond to, and I will use his own term because in those days, in the period which such great significance is being attached to, so I'm going to use his term, the term of coordination. So my question is, and I'm using the witness's term, who did you coordinate on the 12th of July and the 13th of July, 1995 in Potocari among the officers of the command of the 1st Bratunac Light Infantry Brigade, rank, first, and last name, and duty. Furthermore, whose activities did you coordinate on the 12th and 13th of July 1995 in Potocari of the officers of the 2nd Light Infantry Battalion. My next question, or rather what I would be interested in learning about, whose activities did you coordinate on the 12th and 13th of July 1995 in Potocari of the officers of the command of the 3rd Light Infantry Battalion? Who were you the coordinator of in Potocari from the military police platoon on the 12th and 13th of July, 1995? Further, in your testimony in this Honourable Tribunal, the witness said that on the 12th and 13th of July, 1995, the engagement of the military platoon -- military police platoon, one squad was securing General Mladic. They even went to Zepa with him. One squad provided security for members of UNPROFOR in the secondary school centre. One squad was securing the command of the 1st Bratunac Light Infantry Brigade, plus they were engaged at the yellow bridge checkpoint, plus providing security for the Fontana Hotel. He testified that this platoon numbered some 30 or so soldiers, 30 soldiers. I would like to know how is it possible in Potocari on the 12th and 13th of July 1995 there could be 10, 12, to 15 military policemen from the military police platoon of the 1st Bratunac Light Infantry Brigade as testified to before this Honourable Tribunal. I would also like to know, the witness testified in this Court that he subsequently investigated and found out that participating in the mass execution of captured Muslims in the warehouse in the village of Kravica on the 13th of July 1995 in the afternoon, that participating in that execution were two soldiers, members of the Bratunac Light Infantry Brigade and who were locals from the village of Kravica, or what he called the local commune of Kravica. I would like to know if Mr. Momir Nikolic knows their names, their first and last names, and which lower unit they belonged to within the framework of the 1st Bratunac Brigade. I'm talking about these two soldiers. Before this Honourable Trial Chamber, the witness testified that the order to rebury the victims in Glogova was received by Lieutenant-Colonel Vujadin Popovic, chief of security of the Drina Corps and that this order was conveyed to him orally. I would like to know when exactly he received such an order. Where was he when he received that order? How was that order conveyed to him? Was it in personal contact, through communication devices, by courier, or by some other means? He also said that he briefed the commander of the 1st Bratunac Brigade, Colonel Blagojevic, about this. That is, he informed me. I would like to know when this happened, when he did that, the time, the date. Where he did that. Under which circumstances that occurred, that is, was it a briefing, a command meeting, or under some other circumstances? And I would also like to know whether he passed -- allegedly passed this on only to me. And I could select any date, but I'll select one particular one, and I'm asking Mr. Nikolic, is he 100 per cent sure that he met with me and that he allegedly informed me on the 12th of July in the period from 20 to 2100 hours in my office in the headquarters of the 1st Bratunac Light Infantry Brigade? Your Honours, thank you. What I wanted to say to Your Honours I have been able to do and that brings to an end this list of my queries. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Blagojevic. I shouldn't make any comments on your statement, but I think some questions you raised are also the questions in our mind. Well, we'll continue the proceedings. Mr. McCloskey, your redirect.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. And I hope you don't mind if I take some cues from Mr. Blagojevic and ask some of those questions on redirect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: That's your decision. It's your redirect.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. First of all, if we could go to Exhibit P107, an intercept from 13 July. And if we could give the witness the B/C/S version and put the second page of that intercept on the ELMO. Re-examined by Mr. McCloskey:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, you mentioned in your cross-examination that there was an indication in this intercept that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Lack of foundation, Your Honour. There's a lack of foundation with respect to this particular piece of evidence. The Prosecutor needs to lay a foundation, whether this witness is competent to comment on a conversation that occurred with two other individuals and not him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karnavas, I believe that the piece of document was used in the direct examination, and there are some questions asked to this witness, and this witness answered that his name was mentioned in that piece of evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I agree with you, Your Honour. But at this point he's being asked to interpret what two other people are talking about. We do know from the witness list, I believe, that one of the speakers on that intercept will be here to testify. And that matter should be clarified through him and not through Mr. Nikolic who is going to be speculating as to what these two individuals were discussing. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karnavas, I agree with you in certain parts of your intervention, but we could not call Mr. Nikolic again just for this piece of documents in the future. So I'll ask Mr. McCloskey to proceed while bearing your objections in mind on this particular issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall testifying in response to Defence counsel's questions on cross-examination regarding whether or not you had knowledge relating to -- whether your commander met with superior commanders? Do you remember those questions on cross?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You made a reference in answering Mr. Karnavas that there was an intercept that indicated information on that subject. Is this the intercept that you were talking about?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is the intercept that I spoke about during the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you be specific now? What in this intercept were you referring to in responding to Mr. Karnavas's question about your commander meeting with superiors?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Prosecutor. On page 2 of this intercept, there is a question: "Where is your commander?" And then what follows is: "Please, where is your boss?" "Up there, with the people from up there." That's the part I meant. Colonel Blagojevic is Jankovic's commander. He is up there, and what is up there is the office where he is. And now with who from up there? I interpret this as the superior from the superior command. That was my answer, and that is my interpretation now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now if we could go to the Defence Exhibit D21/1 -- sorry, D22/1. That is the October 24th, 1994, order from Mladic. You could put the B/C/S in front of the witness. And now I would provide the Court with what we have in consultation with Mr. Karnavas marked D21/1 bis, which is the revised English version of the translation. If you recall Defence had their own version, and we have been able to now get an English version, and there's no major indication at this point of any major difference. But since this is the official version, I thought it would be a good idea to use it. Now, in paragraph 1 of this document, it talks about the field work of the VRS security and intelligence organs primarily includes intelligence and counterintelligence tasks which depending on the situation make up about 80 per cent of their total engagement. Then it says the remaining 20 per cent of their engagement consists of administrative and staff, military police, and criminal/legal tasks and duties. So your duties on the 12th and 13th, did they involve the military police and prisoners?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Prosecutor. They did include that on the 12th, that is to say, military police duties and also professional leadership over the military police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now you've used this term "professional leadership." And let me go to paragraph 2 of this and ask you a question about that. We in the first sentence see: "The security and intelligence organs are directly commanded by the commander of the unit or institution of which they form part." Now, that is basically right out of the rules that we've already gone over, that first sentence, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then it says: "But with regard to professional activities, they are controlled centrally by the security and intelligence organs of the superior command. This indicates their full independence in the implementation of intelligence and counterintelligence tasks and operative combinations based on the authority set forth in the law and the authority of the appropriate superior organs of the service in applying methods and means of work, in accordance with the law." Are the various -- let me -- you have spoken at length at this point about what you felt were your professional responsibilities related to your task. Can you briefly explain to us again what you mean by those professional responsibilities, how they relate to your superior command, so we can understand how they are different from the other work of the security branch, if they are.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To put it briefly, from a professional point of view, the superior authorities of the security and intelligence organs, say in the Drina Corps, are manifested in the following way: By carrying out first of all this military or specialist training that pertains to security and intelligence matters. Then, what is carried out is approval, giving approval or asking a subordinate to do something in relation to the application of certain methods related to the security organs in their work. So that is how these organs are instructed, that is to say, the organs in the subordinate unit. This is what the superior command does. Then what is suggested is the formation of certain professional organs pertaining to intelligence in relation to collecting intelligence, establishing certain groups, observation points, consultations from that point of view, in relation to the area of responsibility, its specific characteristics, et cetera. However, in principle, the only specific characteristic, the only thing with regard to which the security organ is fully independent and is related to the superior security organ is a request, and everything that has to do with the application and approval of certain methods of work of security organs when carrying out this work actually. Because the security organ in a subordinate command, say, the Bratunac Brigade, does not have the right to introduce certain methods or to apply certain methods in its work before putting a request to the superior security organ, and then this submits a request to a service, ministry, secretariat, et cetera. They come up with their own request in this respect, and then they retroactively give an answer to the subordinate command that sought the request in the first place. So that is the post that comes in envelopes, sealed envelopes, that comes to the security organ personally. It is not the commander or anybody else in the unit that can open this mail. This is a specific characteristic, and this is where there was always confusion quite simply because commanders did not want to understand or could not understand that the application of such methods is approved by the organ. And this is regulated by the rules of service. Now at which level, who approves this, and how, they simply could not live with that, that this mail could not be looked at, that this is a secret, and that is the method of work of the security organs. This would be it in the briefest possible terms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Colonel Jankovic or Lieutenant-Colonel Popovic or General Mladic ever tell you to keep the operation to murder the Muslim men secret from your commander?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may object here for a second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I don't believe that the gentleman indicated that he ever spoke with -- well, I retract that. I withdraw the objection. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me try that again, or do you understand the question?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Mr. Prosecutor, I never received from a superior commander, and also in this case, any order or suggestion that with regard to questions that pertained to my own tasks, to the Bratunac Brigade, to the area of responsibility of the Bratunac Brigade, that I should keep this a secret. I can say to you now -- I mean, I have a document here in front of me that I received from the Prosecution where one can see quite clearly everything that I did. That was in my safe, and also what I left in my safe after I had left. So this communication can be seen quite clearly, how I worked, what I did, and the public nature of my work, and also keeping everything in compliance with the rules of service in the Bratunac Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would it make any sense for the superior command to keep this secret from Mr. Blagojevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Objection. Calls for speculation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. McCloskey, maybe you have to rephrase your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What would be the military -- the consequences of the units that you've described, the elements of the military police, elements of the 2nd and 3rd Battalion, what would be the consequence of those units being used for this operation for two days, three days including the 14th, of the military police, what would be the consequences for the use of those -- if those units were used without the knowledge of your commander?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Again, I'm going to object at this point, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: These are the fundamental issues of the case. If counsel doesn't want to get to them, I think there's enough evidence --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I object to the commenting of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. McCloskey, maybe you could break your question up, establish it step by step, and then come to this final question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Military police were used for three days minimum for a murder operation of this sort --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Objection. There's no testimony that they were used for a murder operation. There's no testimony from this witness that he saw or that he heard military police were actually murdering anyone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I respond to his speeches?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: No, no, no. Maybe the murder is not a good word. Maybe you could ask "used for the operation" in a certain place.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I would not object to that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, this was pure and simple an operation to murder people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I do object to that commenting. What it was, he's indicating what they were doing. The testimony is clear, they were used for security purposes. Now, if he wishes to phrase it in that manner, that's consistent with the testimony, I would have no objections. But to suggest that they were actually out there murdering --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That is not what I'm suggesting. Your Honour, the evidence in this case --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We are not going to spend much time debating on that. Mr. McCloskey, just ask a question according to the way I suggested.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What would the military consequences if commanders weren't told what their troops were doing?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Objection. Objection. It goes beyond the scope of his knowledge. He hasn't been established as an expert in this area. Now he's asking for a legal conclusion from this particular witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karnavas, I think this question is okay because the witness is somebody in the army, has been there for a long time. Of course he will know the consequences if a commander was not told what their troops were doing. Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, might we have like a predicate? Would he know first of all? And then -- I think we are assuming -- I think that had a predicate, do you know -- very well, Your Honour. I accept Your Honour's remarks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, you may proceed, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, do you remember the question?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please repeat it once again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What would be the consequences militarily if a commander didn't know or wasn't told what his various units were doing?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can only say that I can present my personal position. In my opinion, it is absolutely impossible now for a commander not to know what his troops are doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. I'm going to object. It's nonresponsive --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: He's objecting to what I say and he's interrupting the witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: No, no, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It's not nonresponsive to the question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, you have to be very patient. I think I told you that a different cultural background will have a different answer. The witness is going to tell us what's in his mind. He's going to answer this question, but he would like to answer it step by step. We have to be patient.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I will, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nikolic. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have said that with regard to this question, I can present my personal position. I find it incredible that the commander of a unit would not know or would not receive the tasks that his troops were supposed to carry out. Hypothetically, that could happen as well. But right now, I really don't know what the sanctions would be if his troops were to be carrying out certain tasks without his knowledge. I'm really not a military expert. I'm not in that field. Perhaps I can speak about concrete units in my own section, in the police. But right now, I wouldn't like to go into this analysis, and I don't think that I could give an adequate answer because I don't know. I don't know what would happen, what the consequences would be.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Fair enough. You mentioned on cross-examination that an intervention unit from the Bratunac Brigade was working in Potocari, I believe, on the 12th and 13th. Could you tell us in more detail what intervention unit, from what unit?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the 2nd Infantry Battalion, there was a unit. It was not within the establishment of the 2nd Infantry Battalion; that is to say that the battalion according to its formation had a reconnaissance squad. But in this battalion, there was the so-called intervention unit or intervention platoon under the command of Zoran Milosavljevic, nicknamed Kokara. And that's the unit that was in Potocari. In my testimony I said that I saw this officer. He belongs to that unit, and this is from the 2nd Light Infantry Battalion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was this intervention unit and Mr. Milosavljevic doing in Potocari on those days as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I saw when I toured the area was that the unit of Zoran Milosavljevic was trying to secure order there and to provide security for that part of the plateau where people were assembled, about 30.000 of them. And I saw him on the first day, on the 12th, that is. I saw him doing what I said just now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know roughly how many of his unit were with him there?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spoke to Zoran Milosavljevic in Potocari, and he said to me that his platoon got there - I'm conveying what he said - that he had been the region of Caus, and from there his entire platoon went down to Potocari. When I spoke to him then, there were about 10 soldiers from that platoon standing around him. I knew them personally. I know these soldiers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know roughly what the strength of his platoon would have been at that time, aside from these 10 soldiers if, in fact, his entire platoon was in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The strength of that platoon is about 30 soldiers, or rather according to establishment, a platoon has 30 soldiers. I don't know exactly the extent to which it had this kind of manpower. This is a personnel issue. But for me, it was a platoon. That's how it was represented. I don't know exactly whether it had 100 per cent of the required manpower, a bit more, a bit less. I really don't know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the work that you saw this platoon doing and the work you've described the other infantry battalions doing in Potocari necessary to the operation to move the women and children out of town and separate the Muslim men?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, for the most part, that platoon and all the soldiers who were in Potocari were working with the same objective in mind. I could not make any particular distinctions, but the one single objective was to secure the area in Potocari, then to separate the men from the women, to provide security for them, and to remove them to Kladanj, even forcibly. That was the task of all the units that were in Potocari.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. You testified that on the 11th, you received intel information from, I believe, the 2nd Battalion about the number of able-bodied men in Potocari. Can you tell us in particular what form you received that information in, written or oral or courier?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Multiple choice to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Multiple choice to the witness. He's leading the witness. He asked a question, and then he's giving him options.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, this time you are right, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just trying to speed things up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What form did you receive that in?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In relation to the information of that day, in terms of what was going on in Potocari, and from the 2nd Infantry Battalion, I received information in writing. And what I have here in this document that I referred to, I have the following: That this written information came to me from the battalion every day, and I have a document stating that after I had left, they remained in my safe where they had been archived when I left. And the number is 11, here in this document. Daily report from the battalion of the brigade. So this is a document in written form. This report I received in writing. And in addition to that piece of information, I received lots of information in written form from the 2nd Infantry Battalion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, could you provide the document you're referring to the usher so we could get this marked and identified properly. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, what kind of documents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just wish, Your Honours, for you to see, for it to be seen from this document that I received daily reports from the battalion every day. It can be seen that I left them in the safe when I left the brigade and that these are the documents that I had all the time, inter alia, the other documents I had are listed here, too. So this statement refers to daily reports from the battalion. I state -- I claim that I received daily reports from the battalion in writing. But I also received oral reports in that period, before that period, and after that. There is a document, a Prosecution document, that I got in which it can be seen that the daily reports from the brigade remained in my safe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Could we just do it step by step, you know, Your Honour. Lay a foundation to this document. I can only assume that the two gentlemen here, Mr. McCloskey, and Mr. Nikolic, didn't meet last night and that this document -- it seems kind of coincidental that he just happens to have this particular document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This is a big conspiracy, Your Honour. I confess.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: No, no, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I would just like step-by-step process where he can show, demonstrate on the document how it is that he was given -- that that document was given to him on that particular night, that he saw it and he viewed it because it goes directly to the question posed by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, was this document disclosed to the Defence before? Or you just, you know --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I don't know what he's talking about at the moment. I think I know what he's talking about. But if we could get the document, I could find the English translation, we could get everybody a copy of it so Mr. Karnavas can ask the questions. I can also ask him a few more questions about the document. I just wanted to get it marked so we had a number for it at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You have to answer my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Has this document ever been disclosed to the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I don't know what the document is, Your Honour. But we gave everything to the Defence that we gave to Mr. Nikolic, so I believe it must have. But until I see the document, I'm a little reluctant to say. I'm 99.99 per cent sure everyone's got this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Well, again, we need a little foundation. And I think if he's going to be making reference to a document, we should be provided, the Prosecution can look at it without any further testimony, and perhaps give us an opportunity to see whether we have it or give us a copy of it. And then proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Let us have a look at that document. Yes. Do we have the translation of this document? You don't have it at your hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, Mr. Nikolic apparently has brought a bunch of his B/C/S documents that he used in the preparation of his Defence and the preparation of his testimony. I wasn't involved with assembling this material with him. I can only guess that this is a document that we have provided him and everyone else, and it shouldn't take us long to get the English translation of it. I'm sorry, we're all a little tired.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, it's time to have a break. And maybe we'll break until 11.00. And during the break, the Registrar will consult with Mr. McCloskey and Karnavas about this document and to see if there's any translation of this document, whether it has been disclosed to the Defence, and then we'll come back to this document. Yes, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. Might I also ask that if there are any other documents that the gentleman has that he's going to be disclosing at this point as part of his redirect, to save time, he might want to let Mr. McCloskey and myself know what they are so we can expedite the procedure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We'll instruct the Registrar to see to it. We'll resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I've got a translation of this document. It seems to me that the problem concerning this document has been solved during the break. Am I right, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. And just to give a slight background on this, if you recall Mr. Nikolic testified, I think it was on direct, about a commission that was formed and that they destroyed documents. We were able to find this document that refers to the commission after that and got an English version and provided shortly after that a copy to Mr. Karnavas. And so he knows what it is. He has had it. And now that we can see what the document is, this is, in fact, something that's well known -- not for a long time, mind you, but is well known now. And I can, just for the record, try to clear up this issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Could you inform us about the ID number of this document so that we could find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's now designated P94.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may proceed, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you. I think we'll just start with going over a bit this document if we could, and let me give you a copy of the English that we can put on the ELMO. If you could use yours, that would be great.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Nikolic, let me just start with a couple of brief questions. This says -- it's dated 4 April 1997, and it's entitled: "The command of the 501st Infantry Brigade." Can you tell us what the 501st Infantry Brigade is in -- was in 1997.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Prosecutor. The 501st Infantry Brigade is the successor of the 1st Light Infantry Brigade, that is, after the transformation of the army, there was a change of name, and it became the 501st Infantry Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you said the 1st Light Infantry Brigade of Bratunac. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now you had testified about a commission that was formed and about the destruction of documents. Does this -- this document have anything to do with that?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is precisely the document that I referred to in my testimony which contains the documents that I am leaving behind in the safe in the presence of this commission. And the documents that I destroyed are certainly not on this list.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So which of the documents you destroyed are not on this list?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the documents that I destroyed are not on this list.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are any of the documents on this list in existence in the files that we provided you?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can recollect and as far as I remember the contents of all the documents that I received from the Prosecution, I do not see any document on this list which was among those disclosed to me by you. So these are documents that were not contained among your documents.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So do you know what happened to these documents that are listed on this exhibit?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I can say is that these documents are documents that remain within the command of the 501st of the infantry brigade in the safe of the security organ. And my successor may know what happened to those documents. I really don't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This document says that this material was handed over. Who was it handed over to?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These documents were, as stated here, handed over by commission to my successor, Lieutenant Lazar Ostojic from the 501st Infantry Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Number 20, there's some jewellery listed that you personally handed over to the commission. What's that?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Under number 20, it says: "Major Momir Nikolic personally handed gold jewellery from the war booty." And this jewellery is listed from 1 to 6. This is jewellery that was, among other things, handed over to me by MUP bodies when the prisoners who came from the Republic of Serbia were handed over to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, prisoners from Serbia, could you briefly tell us when you got prisoners from Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can, Mr. Prosecutor. We had prisoners from Serbia in the period from the 20th of July 1995 up until and including shall we say the 16th of October 1995. That would be those dates. And I have the records when, who, where were taken over and handed over. I have a complete list of those persons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That was material provided you by the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. McCloskey, I think the redirect should be strictly confined in the cross-examination. The purpose of the redirect examination is to give an opportunity to rebut certain points raised by the cross-examination. I hope you could function within this scope.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned in an answer to one of my questions that this document was some authority showing your receipt of intel reports from the 2nd Battalion. Can you tell us what in this document you were referring to.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Prosecutor. I was referring to the documents in this record under the number 11 where it says: "Daily reports from the brigade battalion." Those are documents and reports received from the battalion sent to the 501st Infantry Brigade after I left.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. On the 11th of July, do you know when you received the written report that you've mentioned getting from the intel section of the 2nd Battalion?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm really not able to tell you exactly at what time a standing instruction issued by me to the intelligence and security organs in infantry battalions was, that in the afternoon, written information be sent in connection with intelligence information collected during the day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who from that battalion, and their name and rank, authored this report that was sent to you on the 11th?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do know, Mr. McCloskey. On that day and on those days, from the infantry battalion for the forwarding of information, Jovanovic Zoran was in charge. I think he's a lieutenant or 2nd lieutenant, and he was acting deputy battalion commander. But because of the situation in that battalion at the time, because of the changes, he had previously been the intelligence and security organ in the battalion. He was -- Milenko Jovanovic was appointed to that position. In the meantime, pursuant to my proposal and the order of the brigade commander, Colonel Blagojevic, Jovanovic was sent to attend a training course in Bileca, and I requested, and this was in agreement with --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. It was a simple question. We don't need to go into too much detail. You can always explain your answer, but I think we got the point.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I apologise, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You heard Mr. Blagojevic's question regarding whether or not you were ever an operations duty officer. We've heard your testimony on that point. Based on his question, do you have any changes to make to your testimony regarding whether or not you were ever duty operations officer?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do, Mr. Prosecutor. That is absolutely not true. Never was there in the security organ a duty officer. So there was no parallel duty service. There was operations duty service in the brigade, and there was duty service in the military police. So those are the only two types of duty service that I knew existed and functioned. I personally, even before Commander Blagojevic and during his stay in the Bratunac Brigade, I was on innumerable occasions the operations duty officer in the Bratunac Brigade. For the sake of truth, let me add that I could, I had approval and permission from Commander Blagojevic when necessary in order to perform my duties to find a replacement, and I could leave. I had that authority, and I want to say that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you receive an order on the 12th to be the -- sorry, let me try that again. Who ordered you to be duty officer on the 12th?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is no order. I was the duty officer pursuant to the plan of duty service for that period. And as I have already said, that plan of duty service is approved by the commander or the chief of staff if authorised to do so. So I was on duty according to the plan of duty service.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Regarding Potocari on the 12th and 13th, you've mentioned the presence of elements of the 2nd Battalion. Did you specifically coordinate with any individual from the 2nd Battalion?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in my testimony, I said that there were two officers present there, Zoran Milosavljevic. I gave him instructions and told him what he should do, how he should secure the area, what his role was, and the like. Similarly, to the soldiers who were with Zoran Kovacevic. I also told them that they should take care of the refugees, assist in their evacuation, and that on that day they should work together with the other units.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Same question for the 3rd Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the 3rd Battalion, on the first day, I saw a number of military conscripts. I didn't have any contact with the commanding officer from the 3rd Battalion. I said that in my earlier testimony as well. But I did see that they were present on the 13th in larger numbers than on the 12th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Given that you have testified that the Bratunac military police platoon had 30 members on -- in the period of July, can you break down for us, for the 12th and 13th of July, as you did in direct, but as concisely as you can, what numbers of military police officers were fulfilling what duties on the 12th.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can tell you approximately. One squad was engaged in securing General Mladic. And in my testimony, I said, if that's what you're referring to -- is that what you meant, that I should go and enumerate them?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, and make sure you tell us how many people are in a squad. So go by numbers, each assignment, each number, so we can see roughly where the 30 are working.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say that. There was one squad which numbers 9 men, was providing continuous security for General Mladic. In my testimony, I said that that squad, on the 12th, when General Mladic was present in Potocari was with General Mladic in his security detail. In view of their participation in Potocari, I mentioned a number that were in Potocari at the time. One soldier was the duty person in the premises of the police. One policeman was on duty at the entrance to the headquarters. He was securing the entrance to the headquarters of the Bratunac Brigade. One military conscript was engaged at the bridge, though this was a permanent task between Bratunac and Ljubovija. Two military conscripts or rather police officers were engaged as reinforcements to the people manning the checkpoint at the yellow bridge towards Potocari. We had two drivers, and that would make about 15 men, including the security for General Mladic who were occupied with those duties. I don't know whether I left anything out. The other police officers -- no, I'm sorry. There were two patrols. One to secure UNPROFOR members, and I don't think I've left anything else out. And I said between 12, 13, or 15 men could have been engaged at that point in time for other assignments. And I said among other things that most of them were engaged in Potocari.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said two patrols, one to secure UNPROFOR. How many men in a patrol? How many men are you talking about there?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two police officers. In most cases, depending on the needs. Sometimes only one, but in most cases while UNPROFOR members were in Bratunac, there were two of them. I apologise. All this is visible from the daily reports of the military police platoon. Their daily engagement for various assignments can be seen from the daily reports that I received from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Those were the -- what we refer to as the "military police log"?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, those are the daily reports of the military police platoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you name the individuals that your investigation identified -- I'm sorry, let me try again. You looked into whether or not there were any Bratunac Brigade members at the Kravica. Do you have -- did you receive any information -- what information did you receive naming any individuals?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: What were the names of the people that he has already indicated? What were the names?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Prosecutor, I spoke in concrete terms about the participation of members of the Bratunac Brigade on the basis of what I subsequently collected as information. So there was Nikola Popovic, who is a member of the military police platoon of the 1st Light Infantry Brigade. And I said that they were locals, that they were born in Kravica. And a member of the 1st Infantry Battalion, his name is Martic, Martic is his surname. I will remember the first name in a moment. Milovan Martic. Those are two members. One is from the military police platoon, and the other from the 1st infantry battalion of the Bratunac Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Regarding the reburial, when as best as you can recall did Lieutenant-Colonel Popovic first contact you about that job?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, in my testimony I said that to the best of my recollection, this was sometime in September, maybe at the beginning of September. But the exact date I really don't know when this was. But in any event, it was in September.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what form did that contact take?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Vujadin Popovic came to Bratunac, and the two of us met in my office in the headquarters of the Bratunac Brigade. On the first occasion, there were other visits in that connection. That was not the only contact linked to this operation with Vujadin Popovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During this first contact about the reburial operation, were there any other people present?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. On that occasion during the first contact, no one was present. I was alone. I am alone in that office anyway, so the two of us spoke together alone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long after you were informed of this operation by Popovic did you inform your commander, Blagojevic?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think this was immediately after. I can't say whether it was a day or two or five hours, but immediately after. When the requests were made to me regarding the operation, I informed Commander Blagojevic on what the demands were, and I conveyed to him what I said in my statement, where the order was coming from and what the order meant. So Commander Blagojevic was informed in due time about everything that was intended to be done in connection with the reburial.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you've described the various units, civilian and military, that were involved in the reburial. But my question is who, if any, of the other officers of the Bratunac Brigade did you specifically inform about this reburial operation?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I informed and discussed this operation with the commander of the military police, Mirko Jankovic, because according to that plan the military police had a role to play. I can speak about that in detail. Also, during the operation itself, when Mr. Jovanovic Dragisa returned from Trnovo, he was the person who knew about the operation and who took part in it. In that period of time, only Colonel Blagojevic, Mirko Jovanovic -- Mirko Jankovic and Dragisa Jovanovic were informed. Apart from them, I did not inform any of the commanding officers in the brigade command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How sure are you that you met with your commander, Blagojevic, on the evening of the 12th of July and informed him of these events we have been speaking about?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sure, Mr. McCloskey, 100 per cent sure that that evening I met with Vidoje Blagojevic, that I informed him about everything that was going on on that day, that we talked about all the matters that I testified about here. I'm 100 per cent sure that that evening I saw Commander Blagojevic and that I spoke to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I don't have any further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Any questions from the Judges? Judge Vassylenko, please. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, in the statement of facts and acceptance of responsibility, you stated that: "In the morning" - it's page 2 of the document, end of part 4 - "in the morning of 12 July, Lieutenant-Colonel Popovic told me that the thousands of Muslim women and children in Potocari would be transported out of Potocari toward Muslim-held territory near Kladanj and that the able-bodied Muslim men within the crowd of Muslim civilians would be separated from the crowd, detained temporarily in Bratunac, and killed shortly thereafter. I was told that it was my responsibility to help coordinate and help to organise this operation." And then you mentioned a number of units which were assigned to or tasked to fulfill this operation, and you coordinated the activity of these units. So these units made up kind of a special task force to implement the operation.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would not call these units special operations task force. These were the existing resources in the territory. That is what I know. And resources came from the main staff, from the commander of the Drina Corps, the Bratunac Brigade, and the other brigade. So it was nothing else, nothing but those units that participated in combat operations. And after combat operations, they happened to be in Bratunac. To my mind, these are no special forces. It was not my understanding that the evacuation was a special task. This meant continuing an operation that had already started. The combat part had been completed on the 12th when the enclave was taken, and then the second part of the operation continued, which meant those activities that I've already spoken about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: And then, when and by whom these units were tasked to participate in the operation.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What was conveyed to me and what I testified about here is that Colonel Jankovic said to me that the units are the participants that are supposed to carry out this operation and take part in it and that they had already received their tasks. This is what I know, and this is what I was told in front of Fontana on the 12th of July in conversation with Colonel Jankovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, whom these units were subordinated to when the operation was underway? And whom these units had to report about fulfillment of the tasks, of their tasks?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These units that were engaged in Potocari, according to the hierarchy, were subordinated to their commanders. Therefore, since these were units from the complete structure of the Army of Republika Srpska, from battalions, brigades, corps, up to the main staff, that is the chain of command and subordination. Depending on the structure they belonged to, they were subordinated to the main staff, to the commander of the Drina Corps, to the brigades that took part in this operation. And they, Your Honour, had their own commanders. Their commanders commanded them. And as far as I know, every one of these structures was supposed to report to their commanders, their superior officers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: And what was your role in this operation as coordinator?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My role, Your Honour, in this operation was the following: The units that were given tasks in these operations were the ones I was supposed to help. I was supposed to establish some contact and some order in the area. I was supposed to try to resolve problems should they crop up, and I was supposed to focus on the main point, and that is to evacuate the population, the women and children, as soon as possible to the free territory under Muslim control. And that part of the men should be separated temporarily, singled out, and transported to the facilities in Bratunac that I already testified about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, was there a division of labour between these units, the units taking part in the operation? Were some units or elements of some units tasked first to mop up and detain the refugees and prisoners; second, to separate able-bodied Muslim men from the crowd; third, to transport women, children, and elderly to the Muslim-controlled territories; fourth, to kill able-bodied Muslim men; and fifth, to bury and rebury bodies of the killed persons?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I cannot give an affirmative answer to your question. I can only tell you that as for the deployment of the units, it's the one I found when I came to Potocari. That is to say, that certain units were at the site where the separation was taking place. Certain units were helping, or rather securing the corridor for the passage of civilians who were singled out for transport. Certain units were helping with the buses. A number of units were linked to the facility where the men were being separated. So I did not take part, and I do not know. I do not know about a meeting -- or rather, at that time I did not know about the meeting where all of this had been planned and where specific orders were issued to these units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, yesterday you testified that your powers included such as to make suggestions and proposals, and if necessary, to issue orders in the sense of having the main say as to what will be done, when and where in a technical sense, in an organisational sense.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, Your Honour, I said that. When I said that during my testimony, I explained it. I explained the action I could have taken. I mentioned the example. For example, when there was a problem with the buses, providing security for them, their passing through the town of Bratunac where a problem cropped up. Then the problem of omissions where people were being separated actually. I was supposed to give suggestions in that respect and to give orders to have things done in a way which would make it possible to carry out the evacuation and the entire operation as efficiently as possible. My powers were within that scope. And I underline once again that immediate command over the units in Potocari was exercised by their commanders who were there, and of course the individual commanding officers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
