utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, in the statement of facts and acceptance of responsibility, you admitted "I coordinated and supervised the transportation of the women and children to Kladanj and the separation and detention of able-bodied Muslim men." And who coordinated and supervised the killing of the separated Muslim men?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, in Bratunac, there was no organised, planned killing. In Bratunac where I was engaged and where the Bratunac Brigade was engaged, that is where the temporarily detained men were kept in the manner which I described. And the operation of killing took place in the Zvornik territory after the captives were transferred to that territory on the 14th of July 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, describing the events which took place in the evening 12 July between 18 hours and 21 hours, you admitted that "it was apparent to me that Colonel Blagojevic was fully informed of the transportation and killing operation and expected me to continue to carry out the duties related to those operations that I had begun that morning." How can you comment on this statement made by yourself?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I can make comments in the following way: On the 12th in the evening, I informed Commander Blagojevic about the general situation and as I put it in this statement of mine. Colonel Blagojevic did not suggest to me at any point in time, nor did he forbid me or issue an order that would be contrary to that, that I should stop doing this, that I should not be engaged in these tasks, or that I was not supposed to do anything about these tasks. So I was given no orders that were contrary to that. Had by any chance the commander of the unit given me the following order: "Captain, you did that. These are not my orders. I do not know about this operation. You should not go on doing that," I could have continued doing that irrespective of his prohibition, but then Mr. Blagojevic, the commander, would the next day or in the forthcoming period simply suspend me from the duty I held. He would have started an investigation. He would have taken measures and asked for criminal proceedings to be brought against me. That evening, after my reporting, after I informed my commander, nothing happened to the contrary, and no order was issued to me, meaning that I should stop doing this, that I should not be engaged in this task. And that is my explanation. And after that, until the operation was over, until the burial and reburial of the graves, several months after that, Colonel Blagojevic never did anything in terms of prohibiting my participation in this or taking proceedings in case I had refused to carry out his orders. No such thing happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, what was the most critical time period of the killing operation?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have partly given an answer that for Bratunac, the most critical days were the 12th and the 13th, and also between the 13th and the 14th, until the transport to Zvornik, that is. The most critical moment related to the killing is one that I'm not aware of because I do not know how, in which way the killing in the Zvornik Brigade started and went on. I just had information that this was going on after the 14th. And we all knew, all of Bratunac knew, all the officers, we all knew that this was going on in Zvornik. But I really don't know about the details in respect of all of this, and I do not know what the most critical moment was in respect of the killing because this was not in the territory of the Municipality of Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Then Mr. Nikolic, you told us that you were a duty officer in the Bratunac Brigade from the morning of 12 July until the morning of 13 July 1995. So it was at the beginning. As you just said, it was the crucial time period of the operation. How it came that you were appointed duty officer in the brigade and being coordinator of the operation?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I explained the way in which the duty service operates in the brigade. That is to say that duty service in the brigade is based on the plan of operations duty, and that is a plan that is made for seven or three days or ten days or even a longer period. I have also said to you that I was duty officer before that and then, and I could have been sent from this duty to other tasks that had greater priority than the duty roster. And that then I would be replaced by persons from the Bratunac Brigade. It so happened according to the plan that I was on duty that day. I was being replaced by colleagues from the brigade. So when this task was being carried out, I had assignments immediately on the morning of the 12th, and this made it incumbent upon me as head of the security of the brigade to do so because it had to do with providing security for the head of the main staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, in your interview given in May year 2003 at the Scheveningen Detention Facility, information report dated 23 June year 2003, page 2, you stated that during one meeting, the attack on Srebrenica was analysed. There was a conflict between Blagojevic and Krstic which resulted in Blagojevic later standing up and leaving the meeting. Can you tell us what caused this conflict.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is an information report, and I know exactly what the issue was, what the question was, rather. And I know what my answer was in respect to this question. Meetings were discussed, and I said that I have information that at one meeting, and I then expressed my fear that I'm not quite sure which meeting this was. But nevertheless, I do have information that at one of these meetings at the command of the Bratunac Brigade, there was a conflict between General Krstic and Colonel Blagojevic. What I heard, what I had received by way of information, was that General Krstic and Colonel Blagojevic had clashed over the way in which the Bratunac Brigade, or rather the battalion of the Bratunac Brigade would be engaged. I did not say that I attended the meeting. I did not mention that in the interview. I did mention the exact date. I was speak being tentatively in those terms that within that period of time, that that had happened as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: But what caused this conflict? Why this conflict arose?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I had by way of information was that General Krstic was unsatisfied with the way in which the battalions were engaged, or rather, the Bratunac Brigade during the attack operations against the Srebrenica enclave and the directions in which they had been engaged. That is what I heard was the reason for this conflict.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Okay. My next question relates to the destruction of the documents. You testified that at -- on 23rd of September, transcript page 49, that you handed over the safe to the chief of intelligence, Major Pajic. And you turned this safe and destroyed the documents. Who ordered destruction of the documents?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I said in my statement and I assert now that with regard to the destruction of documents, a certain number of documents from my safe, I had not received orders from anyone. I destroyed these documents. Simply, the documents that pertained to certain issues related to Srebrenica. I destroyed these documents. I did not receive orders from anyone. And as for the rest of the documents that I handed over, or rather, that stayed in the safe are on this list, are recorded here.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: And Mr. Nikolic, why did you decide to destroy the documents?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, at that time, that period, I was simply afraid of the consequences. I knew what had happened around Srebrenica in that operation. I had certain documents that analysed and gave innumerable names and details, and quite simply I was afraid to hand over these documents to anyone. These were my personal documents. They did not relate to the documents that I as the head of the intelligence and security organ were doing. These documents remained in the safe, and they pointed out all the details, every minute detail related to the operation. And quite simply, I was afraid. I knew that what was underway were searches of the commands by SFOR. I took these documents, and I destroyed them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Can you describe the documents you destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can, Your Honour. Among others, there was my diary which contained everything that was going on in the period while I was in the army by dates, times, names. Also there were many names, many pieces of information that were handwritten, not typed out. So this was the type of document involved. Diary, notes, my opinions, et cetera. That's the kind of document -- the kind of documents that were there and that I burned when I left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Did you destroy any documents containing orders from your superiors and documents signed by yourself?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. Here, on this list it can be seen that I left the orders that came to me because I think there was no need to destroy these documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, can you tell us what civilian bodies have functioned in the Municipality of Srebrenica at the time of the operation.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Bratunac and in the territory of Bratunac, until the operation started, there were authorities that were functioning and that called themselves the authorities in exile, and they had their offices in Bratunac, not in Srebrenica. After the fall and after the liberation of Srebrenica, in Srebrenica a public security station was established straight away. I know that, right after the fall. And I also know, and I have information that after the fall, Mr. Miroslav Deronjic, the commissioner for civilian affairs appointed by President Karadzic, was given the task to establish all the civilian authorities in Srebrenica. That is to say, new authorities in a newly liberated municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: And what was the relationship between you as coordinator of the operation and the civilian authorities in the municipality?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With the civilian authorities in the municipality, I had no special relationship except in one instance when at the request of Major Kingori, it was requested that the water in Potocari be secured. And I called up Ljubisa Simic, the president of the municipality in Bratunac, and requested that water tanks be provided for the people in Potocari. That was my only contact and only request to those bodies. As far as I know, all the other contacts were maintained at the level of General Mladic, Miroslav Deronjic, and the leadership -- the civilian leadership of Bratunac Municipality including members of the leadership from Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no more questions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're welcome, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Vassylenko. Judge Argibay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Nikolic, I first want to ask you a very curious question, because you mentioned your first day that you were talking about the positions of different battalions, forces, et cetera. And you spoke about so-called cockade or star region. Can you tell me what that is.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can, Your Honour. It is a position, a feature, a hill situated in the area of responsibility of the 2nd Infantry Battalion. It is a position at which a certain number of soldiers were stationed from the membership of the 2nd Infantry Battalion. And it is from that hill Potocari can be seen and an area in front of Potocari can be viewed properly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. As I remember, you told us that Colonel Jankovic arrived in Bratunac when Colonel Blagojevic was in the forward command post. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that to the best of my recollection, Colonel Jankovic arrived around the 7th or 8th in Bratunac. And it is true that at the time, the commander, Blagojevic, was at the forward command post at Pribicevac. But let me just mention, I think I failed to mention that in my testimony, and that is that during those days, officers who took part in the operation would come in the afternoon or in the evening when the operations were over for the day. So they would come to the headquarters of the Bratunac Brigade, so I'm really unable to name exactly who they were. But there were comings and goings of participants. I'm not quite sure who, but I do know that they would come to the headquarters of the Bratunac Brigade in the evenings of those days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Who received Colonel Jankovic at the Bratunac Brigade headquarters?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the Bratunac Brigade headquarters, I don't know exactly who received Colonel Blagojevic. I know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: I was talking about Colonel Jankovic.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. I said I didn't know who exactly received him, but I do know that I was within the barracks compound when they arrived.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Who assigned him to your office? Who said he could sit and use your office?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume that he was given an assignment by his commander, and that is General Ratko Mladic who told him to go to the Bratunac Brigade. This is just my assumption. I didn't hear or see that, who gave him the assignment to report to the head of the security and intelligence organ in Bratunac and to be in his office during that time. But I can only assume that. But I can say that as a rule and almost always, officers from a superior command when coming to the command post of a unit or brigade, that they first contact the commander or chief of staff or the operations officer on duty. And after that, having conveyed to the commander why they are there, what their assignment is and what their requests are, after that they are assigned to officers if they are staying there for a while. And I can say with certainty that every arrival to a subordinate unit begins with a meeting with the brigade commander, chief of staff -- or the chief of staff in the absence of the commander, or the operations duty officer if both the commander and chief of staff are absent, which is rare.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: The commander was absent at the time?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the commander was absent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: So you cannot tell who Commander Jankovic presented himself to?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say who he presented himself to. I said the next officer that he should have contacted would be the chief of staff of the brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Was there a deputy commander?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. According to establishment of the light infantry brigade, the chief of staff is also the deputy commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: And who was the chief of staff at the time? Sorry, I can't remember all the names you mentioned, so you just say it, please say it again.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The chief of staff of the Bratunac Brigade and also deputy commander was Major Novica Pajic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Okay. Where was Major Pajic on the 11th July?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I know is what I read from the document, the order. So I don't know -- I didn't know at the time where the chief of staff was. But I read from the document that Major Pajic, according to the assignment, was within the 1st Infantry Battalion at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: So was he in the field or was he in Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I have to tell you that I don't know whether at the time he was in Bratunac or in the field. I just told you that I know that I read in a document that on the 11th, he was engaged within the 1st Infantry Battalion, if you're asking me about the 11th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: When did your commander come back from the forward command post?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, my commander returned in the afternoon or evening from the forward command post on the 11th, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Did you meet him when he came back?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 11th in the evening, I did not meet with Commander Blagojevic in person, nor did I have any personal contact with him on the 11th in the evening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: And you didn't have any contact on the 12th in the morning?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. In the morning of the 12th, there was no meeting, no reporting, no briefing. And there was no meeting in the brigade headquarters, nor did I personally have a meeting with Commander Blagojevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: General Mladic was in Bratunac on the 12th in the morning?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, General Mladic, on the 12th in the morning, he was in Bratunac, and he was also there on the 11th, in the afternoon and the evening of the 11th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: And did your commander went to meet his superior officer from the Drina Corps and from the armed forces of Republika Srpska, that is, the supreme commander in the military field? That was General Mladic at the time.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid I didn't understand the question, Your Honour. I understand the question was whether my commander went to meet with -- that was the interpretation. Could you please repeat your question. What exactly you had in mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Under this hierarchy, usually the one who is under some other and who is at home, and it was Bratunac for the 1st Light Infantry Brigade, is going to meet and to receive and to say "welcome," maybe to his superiors. That's military etiquette, I think. So that why I'm asking if your commander was receiving General Mladic and General Krstic and General Zivanovic, if I don't remember wrongly.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, General Krstic and General Mladic and a group of these senior officers from the main staff and the corps command had been present for days already in Bratunac. As far as I can remember, General Mladic from the 7th or 8th; General Krstic even before that. And according to what I know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt you, but at the time you told us that your commander was in the field. He was in the forward command post. So I was asking when he returned to Bratunac, did he made the honours to these special visitors?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, they were together in the field, in the same field where Colonel Vidoje Blagojevic was, in that same area General Mladic and General Krstic were, and many other officers. They were all in the same place, they were together along that axis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: How many meetings do you know, if you know, was Colonel Blagojevic invited to share with the higher command?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that, how many meetings he was invited to, because these are things that are not passed on to me. These are personal contacts between superior commanders and their subordinates, so I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: You told us during your testimony, I think, that General Zivanovic was the one who told you about the Srebrenica operation, and at one point or other you stated that you either were with Zivanovic's circular group or with Krstic, there was a conflict between the two generals.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I said that there was a conflict between General Zivanovic and General Krstic. And it lasted a long time, and we were all aware of that conflict.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: And were you in the circle or group of General Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I was not within the circle of either of those senior officers because I was a reserve officer with a low rank, and I was not one of the officers who could in any way influence either side. In those days, when General Zivanovic was corps commander, I executed the orders he issued to me. When the corps commander became General Krstic, I again executed orders received from General Krstic as the corps commander. And that was my attitude towards commanding officers, or specifically General Zivanovic and General Krstic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: What about your commander, Colonel Blagojevic? Was he siding with one or the other general?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know that. I don't know what the attitude of Colonel Blagojevic was. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Okay. You told us that the then commander of the Zvornik Brigade - that was Lieutenant-Colonel Pandurevic, if I got it right - was present at a meeting at the Bratunac Brigade headquarters on the night of 11 or 12th July. Did your commander, Colonel Blagojevic, attend that meeting, too?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. As far as I can recollect, this meeting that I spoke about was attended by all the participants in the Srebrenica operation, the offensive on Srebrenica. All the commanders of the units, groups, all the commanders participating in the operations attended that meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: So there were a lot of people there.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were a lot of senior officers there who were participants in that operation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Did Colonel Jankovic attend that meeting?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't remember with precision whether he was there. I know only that many people attended, so I don't know for sure. Possibly he was there. If you're asking about the meeting on the 12th, I think that on that occasion, I didn't attend that meeting. I was not present, but according to the information at my disposal, that meeting was attended only by commanders of assault groups and units that participated in the Srebrenica offensive. And Colonel Jankovic was not one of those.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: The thing is I have a little bit of confusion about the confusion of the names of the units and all that because, for instance, I found in one place that you talked about the 2nd Motorised Brigade. Is that the complete name, or are you referring to another one and I'm absolutely out of the picture?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly, Your Honour, that I didn't tell you the full name of the brigade. I was speaking about the various units that participated in the attack on Srebrenica, and then as far as I know - and I probably mentioned that unit - I don't know its exact name even now. I know it was the 2nd Motorised or Mechanised Brigade from Sokolac or Han Pijesak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Do you remember the name of the commander of this brigade?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was Lieutenant-Colonel -- I can't remember now. I know the lieutenant-colonel personally. I know his first and last name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: In one of the parts of the -- in part of your testimony, and it's page in the transcript 1.640, you said that there was Zekovic. Can it be that person? Because you said: "Commander Zekovic, chief of the 2nd Motorised Brigade." Could it be the lieutenant-colonel you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I think I was talking about Sejkovici, a commander from Sejkovici. I don't think I mentioned Zekovic. Maybe it's an error in the transcript. I don't think such a commander exists by that name. I spoke about a commander from Sejkovici who participated in the operation of Srebrenica and that is Colonel Andric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Is Colonel Andric the same that was in 1999 general?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he is an officer who after the Srebrenica operation became chief of staff of the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Yes, I want some clarification if you can. Remember the clips of the videotape you saw when you identified two persons, one from the Panthers from Bijeljina, and the other one wearing a bandanna probably from the 3rd Infantry Battalion, I remember you said. Remember you saw those videos?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: What were the soldiers doing there?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One of those does not belong to the Bratunac Brigade. He's the soldier known as Gargija. He belonged to the Panthers. And I really don't know what he was doing there. This other one on the photograph known as Lika, I don't know his full name, was present there according to what I saw as an individual. And I really don't know what his concrete assignment was. I saw him on the photograph, and that's all I know about him. And I conveyed my assessment as to what kind of people they were, the information I had about them as a security organ, and that's all I said in my testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Okay. So we are not sure if they were acting under orders in that place, or were they acting on their own, you can say that?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot. Regarding the first one, I can say that he came of his own accord because the Panthers, as a unit, did not take part in that operation. He belonged to that unit, and it was a hundred kilometres from Bratunac. As for the second one, I can't claim anything because he appears there as an individual in the company of this other one who is a member of the Panthers. So I really cannot judge what the two of them were doing there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Okay. When you had some information to deliver or to report to your commander and the commander is not at headquarters, do you have any means to communicate with him?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There is always a line or almost always a line of communications between the commander and the headquarters of the Bratunac Brigade. I personally didn't have any communications device through which I could get in touch. So I personally, Your Honour, didn't have any communications, means which I could use to communicate with the commander directly in his absence. But such communication devices did exist in the communications centre in the headquarters of the Bratunac Brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. But they just tell me we have to have a break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, we'll have a break. We'll resume at 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Judge Argibay, please continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. Nikolic, I only want two or three little clarifications because I have a little bit of confusion with the dates. You told us that you knew from the 12th July that these prisoners were going to be executed and that you were standing in front of the Hotel Fontana before the third Hotel Fontana meeting with Popovic and Kosoric, waiting for the DutchBat representatives and the civilians representatives from Srebrenica to come, and you were already talking about the execution. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, you are right. Everything you said was right in relation to my presence and the conversation that took place and what I knew before the third meeting from the conversation with Lieutenant-Colonel Kosoric and Lieutenant-Colonel Popovic, namely, that I knew what would be done in Srebrenica, who would be transported, and who would be separated from Potocari, temporarily detained, and ultimately executed. That is what I knew because I heard this piece of information from the two lieutenant-colonels in front of the Fontana Hotel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: And at that time, you came with prospective execution sites?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, I suggested a site for temporary detention, and I gave the names of these sites during my testimony. We then had a discussion in front of Fontana about execution sites in the territory of the Municipality of Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: So these executions were supposed to take place in the Bratunac Municipality?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have said during my testimony that we discussed sites for execution, two sites, at that. And I can draw the conclusion that the execution of these people was supposed to be organised in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: And there were no preparations underway for that operation at the time?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, and I did not testify about that particular matter. I don't know whether there were any preparations. At that time, I did not know anything about the executions in Bratunac in greater detail. I don't know if I testified about this, but subsequently, that is to say, after a while, after the operation was completed, I heard, or rather, I received information concerning some action that was taken in the territory of the Municipality of Bratunac with a view to having this execution carried out in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Because if I remember correctly, it was by the night of 13 July that you have this meeting with Colonel Beara and your brother-in-law, I suppose, that was from the municipality, and they decided that the executions would take place in the Zvornik Municipality. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At this meeting, and I know because I was present at the meeting, the main speaker regarding this particular matter, where the prisoners would be going and also the main opposition came from Mr. Miroslav Deronjic, the then commissioner for civilian affairs who had been appointed by President Karadzic. The Muslims who were taken prisoner were supposed to be taken to Bratunac, and in Bratunac, and around Bratunac there should be no execution or killing whatsoever, no way. That pertains to the question that was discussed at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: I see. Can you tell me what were the proposed execution sites in Bratunac, the two you mentioned just now.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Two sites were mentioned; namely, the area of Ciglane, the socially owned company in Bratunac, and the area where the lead and zinc mine is, the lead and zinc mine of Sase in Sase.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: You remember the document that is for identification purposes marked D36/1, the one from Mr. Vasic telling the story of Mr. Kovac coming into -- in contact with General Mladic, Krstic, Beara, and others in - let me find it - Vlasenica. Remember that document?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do. I do remember, Your Honour. I do remember this document and roughly the substance of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: From this document, the impression is that the executions were ordered only on 13 July at about 0700 hours. How come that this gentleman is telling us that the order came after the incident in the Kravica place, detention place, and not beforehand, as you tell us that from the 12th you know about that?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I cannot comment upon the way in which this document was compiled. And also, I cannot comment upon its content and its truthfulness. I really cannot. I really am not capable of making any comment regarding that document in that sense, why it was written then, why it was not written beforehand. I really can't. It's a MUP document, and I don't know how it came into being or when or why something like that was written.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I just have a few questions. The first question is related to Kravica warehouse. In your testimony, which I believe in the page 1.739, you testified that: "As an intelligence officer, it was my duty and within my purview to gather intelligence from such sources as I previously defined as my colleague, or rather, collaborators. At Kravica and throughout the Bratunac Brigade, I had people I worked it, and they would cooperate with the security organ. I really can't bring into the public eye the names of the people I had worked with." Who are those people? If you need, we could go to the private session so that they are not in the public eye.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, there is no need. I shall explain this to you, and I think that we will fully understand each other with regard to this question. In this document that we discussed a short while ago, that is to say the record of the 501st Infantry Brigade, it says under item 1: "Associates of the security organs." Then it also says: "Persons that the security organ uses as a source of information." Further on, it says: "The application of methods of work of the security organs and records of persons." And finally, it says: "The work plan of the security organs, 1 act." Under item 1, the associates of the security organ are associates that the security organ in accordance with the rules of service engages for the needs required by their work in the area of responsibility and in the territory of the unit involved. In this case, the Bratunac Brigade. "The associates or collaborators of the security organs are known by their names and surnames only to the head of the security organ who engages them and selects them. The superior command - that is to say, the command of the corps - is aware of a network of persons who are the collaborators of the security organs, but the corps command does not have the names and surnames of these persons. It has the pseudonyms of these persons, and also the particulars of these persons. As for the information contained in the document informing the superior command about the engagement of such collaborators, in addition to the pseudonyms, there are also defined assignments and the line of work of the security organ collaborators of the brigade." Everything that I'm telling you now is defined by the rules of service of the security organs of the armed forces. I availed myself of this right and obligation that I had. And then there is a further paragraph that relates to persons that the security organs uses as a source of information. It contains the names and surnames of these persons, their particulars, and also a brief description of the way in which these persons are used. In principle, in principle, these persons are engaged on a voluntary basis, and on the basis of their consent to work on compiling intelligence and other information that is important for the security organs. This is defined by the rules of service. The names and surnames of these persons are never revealed, either to the superior commander in the brigade or the superior officer in the professional chain of command, that is to say, the superior security officer. I've already explained what is presented to the superior command. As for the results of the engagement of these persons and the information collected that is of interest to the brigade, that is essential to the brigade and its security, as for this information, the superior officer, the superior commander, is informed through briefing, personal contact, and in other ways. Now, even if I wanted to, I could not give the names of these collaborators I used. I simply do not know them off the cuff. But the list of persons I used as collaborators remained under seal in a sealed envelope in my safe, and I handed this over to my successor, Lieutenant Lazar Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Let me ask you a specific question: In your plea agreement, you took the responsibility of the Kravica warehouse, and it indicates that "Mr. Borovcanin," if I pronounce it right, "was present." And we asked if you knew who participated in that incident. During the direct examination you didn't mention his name. Why?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know whether this was an oversight on my part. But if so, I can tell you now that after information was gathered about this incident, I knew immediately after that, and I can confirm that right now as well, that Mr. Borovcanin was commander of the forces that were in Kravica, that took part in the killings there, and that Mr. Borovcanin was commander of all units of MUP in that area from Kravica to Konjevic Polje. And of course, the units that were in Potocari, or rather the part of the units that were engaged in Potocari. If I said anything to the contrary, I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You said "after information was gathered." What's the source of the information? Can you explain to me?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The source of this information were my associates, my collaborators, who were engaged in the village of Kravica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, another set of questions is about those meetings. I think I got a little bit confused with all those meetings as you said during the questions by the Judges, you could not remember exactly on which day what kind of meeting was held. But please do your best, give us a rough idea on a day-by-day base what kind of meeting was held. Let's begin from 11th of July. So far as you remember, was there any meeting on that date?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, in my testimony so far, I have said that I have a dilemma regarding the meeting that was held at the command of the Bratunac Brigade which was attended by the commanders of the assault groups or the combat groups or the commanders of these groups. That is to say that I'm not sure whether this meeting was held on the 11th or the 12th. But I do know that in that period, such a meeting was held. That was the first meeting. The next meeting, as I've said, I also know that in the morning of the 12th, a meeting was held at the command of the Bratunac Brigade, and I know that what was conveyed to me, and later on I was reminded here through a document that the Prosecutor showed me, that in Bratunac on the 12th in the morning hours, a meeting was held at the Bratunac Brigade headquarters. And the third meeting that I testified about and that I spoke about was the meeting on the 13th at the command of the Bratunac Brigade. I said with regard to that meeting that I'm sure that it was held on the 13th at the command of the Bratunac Brigade. Then in my testimony I said that in the period from when the officers from the corps command came, certain meetings were held. And I know that officers did come to attend these meetings at the brigade command. However, I was not a participant in these meetings, and I don't know the exact dates when they were held. That is what I know. And that is what I can recall.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, in your testimony you said that Mr. Deronjic asked you to take part in a meeting on 13th July 1995. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not what I said, or perhaps it was a slip of the tongue if I said it. I said that as for this meeting with Miroslav Deronjic at his office, that I went there on the request of Colonel Beara after the briefing upon my return from an assignment in Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Why were you asked to take part in that meeting?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, and now, I really have no idea why I went with Colonel Beara. He simply ordered me to go with him. I can just guess in relation to the situation that prevailed in the town of Bratunac. I think that this was one of the reasons why I was supposed to be present there, because questions related to the security of the town, the danger involved, that is what was being discussed. And also the fact that thousands of Muslim prisoners were coming in to town on buses and in trucks, and that this imperilled the town in a way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I'm interested in your relationship with your commander Blagojevic, both working relationship and personal relationship. Can you shed some light on that?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I never had any conflicts with Colonel Blagojevic as a person, not related to the relationship that we had as officers in a command. I've known Colonel Blagojevic all my life. I know the family he comes from. He also knows my family. As officers in the brigade where he was the superior officer and where I was his subordinate, we had very correct relations in terms of cooperation and, generally speaking, in terms of carrying out the tasks that were set before us. What I wish to say is that Colonel Blagojevic, to a large part, or for the most part, respected proposals that were made for the use of units concerning which I made proposals in accordance with the relevant regulations, and I can say that we most often did not agree only in one single segment. And that has to do with using the military police platoon. There were certain disagreements on that score in the following sentence: I insisted that the military police platoon should be engaged in military police tasks. The commander of the brigade on several occasions issued orders to use the military police platoon contrary to the proposals that I had made. I will give you a concrete example. For instance, Trnovo, where the Bratunac Brigade was engaged. After the brigade commander passed a decision to use the military police platoon in such a way, or rather, part of the military police platoon, I used that part of the platoon to carry out this task. The commander personally went with them to have this combat assignment carried out in the area of Trnovo. And then when they got there, he had a problem because he had engaged them for that particular task. And this problem was contrary to my original proposal. After that, after the problem that was caused by this engagement which was contrary to the proposal I made in respect of the use of this unit, then Commander Blagojevic called me from Trnovo asking me to come to Trnovo which is 180 kilometres away to resolve this problem with this squad of the military police which had been engaged on his orders and not in accordance with my proposal. And of course, I got into the car then. I went there, and I resolved the problem in the way in which such problems are resolved, by issuing orders, not beseeching people. I am saying that even in Trnovo, the commander had all the necessary resources for resolving the matter. He had a battalion of the military police from the Sarajevo Majevica Corps [phoen]. He could have issued an order to disarm these ten men. He could have issued an order to have these ten men detained, and he could have resolved the problem, not engage me for that particular matter. So this is a concrete example of when we did not agree. And there is one thing where we absolutely disagreed. Can I tell you about that as well?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I just asked you generally, you know. There's no need to give me the concrete examples unless it's related to that critical period. Is it related to that critical period? What I mean is from the 6th of July to the 17th of July.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. My last question is that throughout your testimony, you continuously mentioned that the person you were responsible to or is your direct commander is Mr. Blagojevic. But we heard very few evidence that during the period, from the 6th to 17th of July, there are a lot of contact between you and Mr. Blagojevic. My question is during that period did you receive any order or instructions from your commander, Mr. Blagojevic?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my testimony, I said when I did receive certain assignments. I mentioned the dates. That was in this period at a briefing prior to the attack, sometime between the 3rd and the 5th of July, when I was given one of my assignments. And also, after my informing Commander Blagojevic on the 12th, when he did not oppose, and my understanding was I had his agreement for continued engagement. And again on the 13th, after the morning briefing when I went to execute the tasks that had started on the 12th in Potocari. True enough, Your Honour, in that period of time, there were no regular meetings that we usually held. There were no briefings. And why there were no documents or records about orders issued is explained by this, by the fact we didn't have regular meetings, regular briefings at which orders are issued and then the commander is briefed about the execution of those orders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Any questions out of Judges' questions? Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If I could make just one clarification on your last point, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: One of the exhibits, the meeting notes of the command meetings that we will be offering into evidence has a meeting where I believe Mr. Blagojevic is present, and Mr. Nikolic is issued an order to go to Potocari to do something. And that will be in the exhibit as we offer it. But aside from that clarification, unless you want me to ask him about that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, you have to put it in the form of a question rather than you yourself explaining to us. Further examination by Mr. McCloskey:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, do you recall the command meeting notes that I just spoke of?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Prosecutor. If you're talking about the notes in the preparatory stage for the attack.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was that what you are referring to where you said that was at one point where your commander had issued you a task?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is the note on that meeting when, among others, I received an assignment, too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember what that task was?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The task was for me in that period to ensure a megaphone and to find the most favourable position in the area of the 2nd Infantry Battalion that can best be heard in Potocari.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was that about?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I can say now is that the aim was probably during the attack, should the need arise, for the Muslims to be called to surrender. And from those documents, the task is not quite clear to me either. But that is the only possibility. I can't see any other.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Nothing further, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Karnavas. Further cross-examined by Mr. Karnavas:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you carry out that task?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, as far as I can recall, in that period of time, I never had the need to make any announcements from the yellow bridge. There was no need for me to ensure a megaphone. There were plenty in the brigade headquarters that had been seized from the international organisations. And among the other equipment seized there were megaphones.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you again the question. Do you recall my question?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karnavas. I do remember your question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you answer it, please. Did you carry out that task? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not, Mr. Karnavas, because there was nothing for me to execute.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you asked about this by the Prosecution during the proofing sessions or at any other sessions?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, Mr. Karnavas. We spoke about many things, including that, so I don't know any longer what exactly the Prosecutor asked me. We discussed all kinds of things, including reports, briefings, and everything else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, with respect to this particular order, did he ask you to give some explanation? Yes, no, or maybe?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not an order. These were assignments issued, assignments defined at the briefing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Did you discuss the assignment, the one we're discussing right now? Did you discuss that with the Prosecutor during the proofing sessions? That's what I'm asking.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think we did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was your -- what do you mean "you think"? You either did or you didn't, or you don't recall right now? Which of the three?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, I said that we did discuss all documents, including that document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now you no longer think; you know that you discussed it.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you for that straight answer. Now, could you please tell us what exactly you told the Prosecutor at the time that you discussed this particular assignment. Concretely tell us.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said more or less what I just said here in this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which is?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean now? The contents of what I said?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. What exactly did you tell the Prosecutor? Did you tell him, for instance, that you recall seeing that assignment? That you didn't carry out the assignment because of other reasons? What exactly if anything did you tell the Prosecutor regarding this particular assignment?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told the Prosecutor that on the basis of what it says in the report, I don't know what the gist of that assignment was, and that I assume that the aim and purpose of my engagement was what I said a moment ago, and that is should at a particular point in time I be engaged to call on them to surrender with the help of a megaphone. That's what I said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall receiving that assignment? Today, do you recall receiving that assignment from your commander?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I recall that assignment, only -- or rather, I remembered it once I took the report to read it because there were so many assignments that I really can't remember each and every detail and each and every assignment. But I was reminded by it, and I know that I attended that meeting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So it was after your memory was refreshed through your lawyers with the documents presented to them by the Prosecutor that you recall the assignment?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I do have one question with respect to the meeting that was raised by Judge Argibay. You indicated today that Mr. Blagojevic definitely, or at least that was the impression that I got, that he definitely attended this meeting of commanders, but you can't recall whether it was the 11th or the 12th. Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, I said that that meeting was attended by commanders of the assault groups, and as far as I know, all commanders who participated in the attack on Srebrenica and that that meeting was held in the Bratunac Brigade and that I am certain if they were all there, that Commander Blagojevic was there, too. That is what I said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And you're certain because you saw Colonel Blagojevic coming out of the meeting?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am certain because if this was a meeting of the commanders of assault groups, because I knew -- I heard afterwards what had happened at that meeting and what the discussion was that they held.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, is that the meeting where you claim there was this argument between General Krstic and Colonel Blagojevic, in the presence of General Mladic and Colonel Blagojevic just up and left the room? Is that the one we're talking about?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was speaking of the meeting with the commanders of the assault groups. And according to my information, what was discussed were future combat activities and the continuation of the operation against Zepa. Now, whether other matters were also discussed and what was discussed, I said that I wasn't present at that meeting, and that I did not know the details as to who said what. I just conveyed the main thing that I heard about that meeting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever tell the Prosecutor that there was a meeting where in that meeting, there was General Mladic, there was Krstic, there was Colonel Blagojevic, and others. And in that meeting, in the presence of General Mladic, there is this argument between Colonel Blagojevic and his commander, General Krstic. And during that meeting, Colonel Blagojevic just walks out of the room. Did you ever tell this to the Prosecutor? Yes or no or I just don't recall. Which of the three?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we spoke, I told the Prosecutor that I remember one of those meetings at which there was this conflict between General Krstic and Colonel Blagojevic. And I said that I know that I heard from Colonel Blagojevic that the two of them quarrelled, rather, there was a scene after which Colonel Blagojevic offered his resignation and walked out. It was along those lines that the Prosecutor and I discussed the matter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as I understand it, you also indicated at that time that this was in the presence of General Mladic, who was chairing the meeting apparently, or would have been chairing the meeting considering he was the supreme commander.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that I didn't say that. I said that when we discussed that meeting, that General Krstic was there, and that the conflict arose between the two of them. I think that in connection with that event, I did not enumerate all the commanding officers who were present in the command of the Bratunac Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. There are two questions that I would like to ask that were raised -- that were based on the redirect, if that's permitted. If it's not, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, generally speaking, you have to ask the questions within the scope of judge's questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour. That's why before I asked them -- if I can just tell you what the questions are, and then you may decide.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: One has to do with the gentleman named -- who is nickname is Kokara, a rather colourful character that was described as being seen. I would like to know whether that gentleman is on the video, one of the videos that Mr. Nikolic has seen. And is it not a fact that he has had this gentleman arrested, and so there's a personal history between Kokara and Nikolic. That's the one question. And then the other one dealt with a clarification, and that is the gentleman has indicated today, as in the past, that he received his orders from Colonel Popovic regarding the reburials sometime in September. And I believe it's the beginning or middle of September. That's the ballpark figure. We do have a document that shows that asanacija was referred to in the meeting on the 16th of October. And my question was -- today he indicated that he notified his commander after Colonel Popovic informed him, which would be sometime in September. My question would be: Was this another one of those meetings where it was four eyes and four ears only, because then there would appear to be at least no other verifiable evidence to substantiate, other than this gentleman's statement as to whether that meeting did, in fact, take place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, I'm afraid you could not ask those questions. Maybe the second question is underlying. I think Judges raised it, but the sense and direction is different with yours. But anyway, this witness gave his evidence today here. And you have the full opportunity to verify his testimony at a later stage and call the other witnesses or in your case in chief at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, just one question in the context of the questions put by His Honour Judge Vassylenko. Further cross-examined by Mr. Stojanovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Nikolic, in answer to a question by Judge Vassylenko, you said that before the handover of duty, you destroyed most of your personal documents, your diaries, notes, or your opinions or reflections. Among those documents, was there a single document related to the reburial activities?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, among those documents, there was an official report that I compiled after completing that operation, and it was destroyed. And as you can see from these minutes, there is an item regarding consumption of fuel. So only my official report was destroyed, my own analysis of that whole operation. And everything else stayed behind in the safe. You have here a list of what remained in the safe.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So my question is why did you destroy that official report in view of the fact that you said that you destroyed these documents generally because you said you were afraid that there were a lot of names and you were aware of searches in brigade headquarters? So can this explanation be used to support what you said yesterday, that this was probably a secret operation?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, I can give you a very frank answer to this question. I destroyed those documents which compromised both me and the Bratunac Brigade. So I destroyed that particular document that you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. At this stage, are there any documents to tender into the evidence? Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I have about ten documents. There are several others that we discussed, but for a proper authentication of those military documents, we will be providing that through the normal course. And I can just briefly go over these ten.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: P81, that's the compilation of the plea agreement and material associated with it. P82 is also part of that plea agreement material. P83 are the JNA brigade rules. P84 are the JNA rules of the security organs. P85 is the map showing the brigade's area of responsibility. P86 is the aerial photograph that the witness marked. P87 is the aerial photograph of Bratunac town that the witness marked. P88 is the videoclip of the arrival at the Hotel Fontana. P89 is the videoclip of General Krstic and Zoran Kovacevic doing their press interviews in Potocari. P90 is the videoclip of the people coming in to Potocari, the fellows with bandannas. P93 is the videoclip of the soldiers of the Bratunac Brigade that are along the road. P94 is that Bratunac Brigade document relating to the destruction of documents. And that is my one exception. Since the witness seemed to be so familiar with that document, I think that by his own testimony is probably sufficient to authenticate it. And the other exhibit is a matter of a private session exhibit, P95. And the rest, we'll be providing detailed information on where these documents came from. They mostly were seized from various searches.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Any objections? Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. With respect to P83 and P84, it is our belief that the documents tendered by the Prosecution were incomplete, were not complete. We didn't use those rules; we provided our complete set of rules. So I would prefer, of course, for the Trial Chamber to have the complete set, and I brought this matter to Mr. McCloskey's attention. So either both sets can go, or one could be replaced for the other. So with respect to P85, I guess I'm drawing a blank over here as to whether this map was actually used. And I guess I'm -- and again, I'm not stating that it wasn't. But if I could have my memory refreshed. As far as all the rest, I have no objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. McCloskey, how about the document P85, the map?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: My memory -- I think you asked me if he could look at a map, and I found a map, and he pointed out a few things on the map. It's the map of along the road, and I don't know. I know our recollections may be fuzzy, but I remember you asking me that. It's a small map that shows the basic area, and he pointed to it. Judge Argibay, I see she's got that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: My memory is refreshed at this point. And I have no objections, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we have no objections regarding the exhibits tendered. But we would suggest that it would be more appropriate to admit the entirety of the rules that were referred to here, bearing in mind our own cross-examination when it was stated that security officers could not be duty officers. We have no other remarks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. President. We missed one. It's a videostill of Zoran Kovacevic in Potocari. It's when everything broke. And I just had him circle it, if you recall, and circle the person on it. That is also an exhibit, P96.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I guess there's no objections because I think it's a clip from the documents we have already admitted into evidence; that is, P22. Right?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. I see no objections. So those documents are admitted into evidence. And as for the documents P83 and P84, we hope that the Prosecution could submit us with a complete set of that documents, because really we just have the part you used.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Absolutely, of course, Mr. President. We've got the complete translated set, and we'll make sure you get all of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Well, Mr. Nikolic, thank you very much --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry. At this moment, are there any documents for the Defence to tender?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I just received your list, amended list.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes. And it may need to be amended again. Yes, Your Honour. D12/1, we did discuss that, so I would ask that that be admitted. D15/1. D16/1.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We don't have his amended list, and it may get complicated --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Sure, sure. I think there are so many lists flying. Final, final, final lists.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I might have that. Janet just pointed out to me that maybe I do have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It's dated 30 September 2003.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, that's the one I've got.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Let me go back. D12/1. D14/1, I bypassed that the last time. That's the intelligence support of the armed force JNA manual. D15/1. D16/1. Okay, on D17/1, we haven't been able to locate it yet. And I guess what my position would be, at this point we're not going to tender it -- we're not going to move it into admission. But I did speak with Mr. McCloskey, and we are trying to solve that problem. But I can assure the Court as an officer of the Court that we have never received any official documents outside of Mr. McCloskey. And had we received such a document, I would deem it physical evidence which I would be duty-bound to turn over to the Prosecution. D18/1. D20/1. D21/1. D22/1. D23/1. D24/1. D25/1. D26/1. D27/1. D28/1. D36/1. D37/1. D38/1. With respect to D39/1, of course, that's sort of an issue of contention as far as whether the gentleman should be coming here to give live testimony or whether if he should be moved into 92 bis, and of course I believe after yesterday I made a compelling reason why he should be coming in here live versus that coming in here under 92 bis. And then D40/1. D41/1. And finally, it just occurred to me as I was going through all of this, I would just like to make sure because the gentleman has given various statements and has had briefing notes, with respect to Mr. Nikolic, everything that he has given the Prosecutor from his statement back in 1999 to the statement of facts and acceptance of responsibility to the additional information or the information report from Mr. Bursik to his statement of -- that he gave subsequently thereafter and all proofing notes also be moved in because we refer to all of it. And I think that it's necessary. So when it comes times for us to argue our cases, we then have all of these sources of information, provide them -- collate them into our arguments with respect to the finding of facts the Court needs to make.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. As for D12, I would object. It seems to be a letter from a police department. It's not an official document. I would object to it coming for the truth of the matter in it. It's unclear, this area, whether this is a criminal conviction, some sort of administrative thing. It's very unclear, and without official documents, I think this just muddies the water. I have no problem with P83, the brigade rules, or D14, the intelligence support. D15, the service regulations of the military, no problem. No problem. D16, the July 2nd order of the Drina Corps, that is a -- I have no objection to that. We would be offer the authentication of that later. But if it's simpler to come in now, I don't really care how it comes in. I know that is an authentic document. We are working with Mr. Karnavas on D17, on the 5 July document. It appears genuine to us, and I'm sure we'll track it down. I hope we'll track it down. D18, the Bratunac Brigade search, no objection. Again, we will be providing the authentication for that. D19, this health centre letter, again, this is a hearsay document related to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: It's not tendered.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sorry. Thank you. D20, we get into these business records of that company relating all those issues. I would object to those as all hearsay, of little relevance, and not any probative or substantive value. And that is D20/1, D21/1, D22 -- I'm sorry. D22 is the headquarters of the RSA instruction. That's the 24th document. No objection to that. And we just have our -- the two translations of that document. And then D23 through D27 are those documents related to the companies which I don't think are helpful or relevant or substantial. D28, the 13 July command of the Drina Corps search, no objection. I think the next one is D36. Your Honour, this is a letter from Mr. Vasic who at the time of the events as we have learned was the head of the -- what's referred to as CSB Zvornik. He has been interviewed as a suspect several times by the Prosecution. That material everyone has. In the process of his various interviews, he provided us with this letter. And it's basically him writing a letter about what Kovac, who was the acting minister of interior at the time, what Kovac told him that Kovac heard Mladic say. So it's the most quadruple hearsay imaginable, and as a result for the purposes of questioning during cross-examination, no objection. But as a substantive document that has any kind of weight or credibility, I would object. Now, the statement of Mile Petrovic, again, a statement to be used for cross-examination or to impeach the witness, I have no objection for it being used at that point. But a document to come in substantively is, I believe, against the rules. It should either come in as 92 bis or the person should testify. So I would object to both of the statements of Mile Petrovic, D37/1 and D38/1. Now, the materials related to the statements of Mr. Nikolic, it's my understanding that these sorts of statements from witnesses the Court did not want to be admitted into evidence. And so I would like to be consistent for this witness as well. If -- because of his unique situation, if the Court deems it appropriate to have all these statements, I wouldn't object. But I think it makes sense that we remain consistent throughout.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Maybe you should have something -- so, you finished?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, that's it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Well as for Document D12/1, we believe that is a police document. And there's some relevance in this case, so it's admitted into the evidence. As for the D17 and D18, the Prosecution promised us to work with Mr. Karnavas to find the source of these two documents. And whenever they establish the source of these two documents, we will admit them into the evidence. But not at this moment. D20, admitted. As for the documents D21, D22 until 27, we believe that those documents have some relevance to the credibilities of this witness. As for how much weight we would like to attach to these documents, that's another matter. So those documents are admitted. D28 is admitted since there's no objections. D36 is admitted. D37 until D41 are not admitted into the evidence because they are the statements of the witnesses. As our practice, we do not admit those previous statements into the evidence. It is so decided.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I believe as to 40 and 41, the Prosecution had indicated rather than bring the individual here, that they would not object to the statements coming in, under 92 bis I would take it. As far as 38 -- 37 and 38, I would totally agree. And in light of the importance of this particular witness, and the upcoming events with respect to Mr. Nikolic, I would request that Trial Chamber exercise its powers under Rule 98 and that Mr. Petrovic be brought here to testify as a witness on behalf of the Trial Chamber. It's obvious that he's willing. He's been around. I think his testimony would be extremely important prior to the sentencing of Mr. Nikolic. And I have noted today from the Prosecution that they do intend to call very shortly the only other potential witness on that occasion, and that is Mirko Jankovic. And I've looked through the statement of Mirko Jankovic. He doesn't recall any of the events that this witness has testified. However, he does comment with respect to Petrovic and describes him as an honest man, an honest and a decent man. So I think in light of that, Your Honour -- and I agree with the ruling that the statements should not come in at this point. But given the critical importance of this particular witness, at this juncture, I would prefer for the Court to exercise its discretion as at the present, and I'm sure the Prosecution would not object to it, to bring the gentleman as quickly as possible. And I know it would be somewhat of an interruption in the Prosecution's case. But I think this is an issue that is relevant. Somebody is being accused of killing six individuals, and there's no other evidence other than this gentleman's testimony. But we do have an official statement given to the Bratunac police. We do have another statement, albeit to my investigator, and we also have a witness by the Prosecution who doesn't-- in his interview does not recount this event ever happening. So I think prior to Mr. Nikolic being sentenced I think this is important because again, it would be a violation of the plea agreement if it turned out that that information was false. It would also be perjury. And I think that is something that the Court can consider in aggravating the sentence well above the plea agreement that was arranged. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Briefly, Your Honour, there's nothing to stop Mr. Karnavas from calling this witness himself in these proceedings. That is what, I believe, is appropriate. And of course, perhaps at the end there may be suggestions of Court witnesses. But I think as the system goes, he can perfectly call this person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, we'll consider the requests from Mr. Karnavas. We couldn't make a ruling on the spot today. Yes. Mr. Nikolic, thank you very much for coming to give your evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours, for hearing me out, for having the patience to hear my testimony over the past eight days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. And the guard will show you out of the room.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: As for this afternoon's hearing, we are going to hear Mr. Obrenovic at 4.00 in this courtroom. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sorry, from 4.00 until how long?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Until 5.30.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: The hearing is adjourned. --- Luncheon recess taken at 2.19 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, good afternoon. Before we start, are there any matters that the parties would like to address to us? Yes, Ms. Sinatra.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
