utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I have filed a motion that I think requires an immediate ruling from the Trial Chamber. But if you want me to discuss it, I'd like to go into private session since the document was filed confidentially.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I acknowledge that this motion for the certification, but I just received it 10 minutes before 4.00. I did not have a chance to read it. And Ms. Sinatra, I can assure you that we'll consider your application. And before we make any decisions, I think the Bench's decision we made this morning will be valid.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Just for the Court's information, I have consulted with the Prosecution about when they think these documents might be translated. And I have been assured that they can't give us a time frame until tomorrow. So I'd just like the Court to know tomorrow that I have been trying to seek an answer to that so that we can figure out how to solve the problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your effort. This is also the question would like to know. Are you going into the details of this motion?

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Your Honour, if you haven't had a chance to read it, I don't know. We won't have a chance to take it up this evening prior to Mr. Obrenovic's testimony. But it's the same arguments that I've put forward to the Trial Chamber with the exclusion of the fact that there is no definite time when the translations might be completed. There are confidential documents attached to this. And the Chamber does have a chance to review this, I would like to go into private session before the 5.30 deadline, if possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You know -- you mentioned that there's nothing new in these filings.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, other than my arguments before, it's the same argument that I am asking for you to certify for the Appeals Chamber to decide on an emergency situation. But there is an additional aspect because the Trial Chamber denied my request for the Zvornik Brigade SFOR documents yesterday, and I just wanted to clarify that I'm only requesting these documents if they are in the possession of the Prosecutor, which, you know, they have been disclosed a lot of these documents that were seized. If they have the duty shift book for other months, we need it cross-examination, examination of Mr. Obrenovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, could I turn to Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, there is a collection that we have all been referring to as the "SFOR" collection. That is a collection that was seized a few years ago by SFOR. They did a rough scanning of it, the United States army did. They provided us with electronic copies and returned the originals to the Republika Srpska authorities. And we spent several weeks with the United States trying to make these things searchable. They are roughly searchable. There's about 250.000 documents in this electronic thing, 18 CDs. All those have been provided probably years ago to everyone by now. This is the collection that I believe the Blagojevic team was able to find the October 24th document relating to the security instructions from Mladic. We had not found that ourselves. It can't be found by searching, unfortunately. You have to go through every document. So I applaud them on being able to find that because we hadn't been able to. Now, having said that, counsel has all these documents and has had the same opportunity the Blagojevic team has. And we have searched and searched and searched for anything relevant that we could find. And as I'm sure the Jokic team has. We have no knowledge that there is any logbook or a copy of a logbook in that material. And that's -- this is material that counsel's had for a very long time. And we have been, you know, looking for the logbook since it was mentioned by counsel a while back. And it has been -- I have questioned Mr. Obrenovic and his counsel about that, that is the subject of the proofing notes. We don't have it, and they don't have it. And according to Mr. Obrenovic, it was not one of the documents that he was able to obtain before his arrest. So no one has it. No one knows where it is. And everyone's been trying and making all the best efforts possible. And that's about all I can say about that particular document that she is interested in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sinatra.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I would just like to clarify, I know that the July duty shift book is missing, so just to prove the procedures, normal procedures of the Zvornik Brigade, we asked for June and August. And if they have June and August, or any other month of a duty shift book from the Zvornik Brigade, we're asking for disclosure of it. The documents that he's talking about were given to us on CD, of course, the Blagojevic team has Zylab. We don't have the ability to search these documents efficiently, and they are gigantic CDs. And when you do a search, you can't come up with -- it doesn't say duty shift book. The terminology is something totally different so we're not able to find it. I think I'm just asking for a confirmation from the Prosecution that either they have looked for another duty shift book in their documents, they have -- I know they don't have a July duty shift book because we have already come to that conclusion in our discussions. But if there's an alternative month that we can use, that's what I'm requesting. It says June or August, but I'll take any month in the 1995 period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I think that Mr. McCloskey has already answered your question. I think your team met with the difficulty in searching out of those documents. It's the same on the Prosecution side. The Prosecution has already disclosed all those documents to your side, and it's your responsibility to find them.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Your Honour, my question again is just a confirmation. I don't think that it's in the documents that they gave me. Because what they think I'm asking for is a book that's missing. I'm asking if they have some evidence of a duty shift book for any other month in 1995. And I will accept the Prosecution's answer. If they say they don't have it, then we'll move forward. But I'm just asking for a confirmation one way or the other from the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, the vast majority of material we have from the Zvornik Brigade was obtained in a search of that brigade in 1998, I believe. That material, we have the original documents for. It was very carefully indexed by this team, and that index has been provided. And all the scans of all those documents have been provided on CD which is searchable. And they have had that for, I think, years now. Now, this is the first I've heard of that they want other books. We've always worked well with them and tried to find things that they may not be able to find. And we will, if she is looking for June, we'll make sure we take a look for June. But again, that's about all I can say. I'm not aware of a June book, or I'm not really aware of exactly what book she is talking about. As you'll hear, there's a lot of books. And we'll try to make that as clear as possible. But we'll work with them as we always have and we'll try to sort it out best so that we can find these things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I will try to get with the Prosecutor after Court today and see if we can find that. But also I think it's really important that maybe the Trial Chamber take a moment to look at the request for certification because it requests a stay of the proceedings before Mr. Obrenovic testifies. I know the Trial Chamber has ruled on that, and since I had a ruling on my request to the Trial Chamber, I'm now asking for a certification to appeal the issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much to draw our attention to this motion for certification, and also I noticed that the proceedings this morning was attached. Am I right? At the back of this motion.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: It was the proceedings from yesterday evening, before we broke, and also the confidential information. Although the Prosecutor has not asked us to keep it confidential, I believe that it should be so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Ms. Sinatra, as I told you that the Trial Chamber has made a decision concerning your two motions already, and yesterday we denied your two motions. And today you filed this certification for appeal, we want to know whether in these motions there's something new that we should consider. But if you inform us there is nothing new in this motion, I'm afraid that we could not accommodate your request.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Your Honour, the new information was the document that I filed with the Trial Chamber this morning. I don't know if you've had a chance to review the proofing notes. But also, because there's a different standard to be set under Rule 73(B) which is asking for certification, it's to determine whether the denial of the continuance of the live testimony based on the new disclosures of potential documents that have not been translated, based on the 19 new pages of debriefing from the witness who is about to take the stand, that it does affect the fair and expeditious conduct of the proceedings and the outcome of the trial. So the test under 73(B) is different from the request we made earlier. And other than the fact that we have consulted with the Prosecution, the documents have not been reviewed by the Defence. Mr. Stojanovic has not had been opportunity other than a cursory review of 70 documents to determine how relevant they are. We really don't believe that it's going to be in the best interests for the defence of Mr. Jokic to proceed with the direct examination of Mr. Obrenovic at this time. And there is no new evidence here other than what I've presented. I think we just need the Trial Chamber to grant or deny the certification and the stay of proceedings one way or the other. I do hope the Trial Chamber has reviewed the document that we filed this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Very briefly, Your Honour, the proofing notes that counsel's speaks of -- the proofing notes that was provided on Friday, last Friday, so that is not new. Also, Mr. Stojanovic came over Monday night and was able to go through the new documents, and we photocopied him all the ones that he picked out from the new documents. And so I just wanted to make that clear for the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: And could I ask you a question. How soon could we get the translation of those documents which you believe that is most crucial?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We have identified the new documents, and we have identified with the help of Mr. Stojanovic the ones he's interested in, so by priority of what they are interested in we have asked a very urgent request from the translations unit. And I don't have a time frame yet. Mr. Waespi is working on that. Well, he should be working on it. I see he's behind me at the moment. But as you know, the translation has been excellent in that regard in helping us out. So hopefully, very soon. But there are a -- you know, a fair amount of pages, as counsel has said. And I would have a better idea for you tomorrow, I hope.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: And how many pages altogether?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It looked like about 50 to 70, I think. But again, I have not had time to go through them. Those were the new materials. How many Mr. Stojanovic actually picked out is something like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I leafed through this motion, and I believe this only consists of four pages, and the others are the annex. And after consultations with my colleagues, we are going to deny that motion for the certification of appeal. As we made a decision yesterday, the Trial Chamber suggested to the counsel for Mr. Jokic that they might have another opportunity to visit this issue at a later stage, which means that they could have the opportunity for further cross-examination of Mr. Obrenovic. In the meantime, we urge the translation section to have those relevant documents translated as soon as possible so the Judges will be at a better position to see whether they are of crucial importance or not. It is so decided. Could we have the witness, please. In the meantime -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I was just going to call Dragan Obrenovic, the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: In the meantime, we notice that Mr. Obrenovic's Defence team is here. And this Trial Chamber allowed you to be present to observe the proceedings. But I have to remind you that you are not a party to these proceedings; you are just counsel for Mr. Obrenovic. So there's no right on your part to make any intervention during the whole proceedings. You might consult your client on the legal issues, but not on the factual issues. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President. Good afternoon. Could you please state your name and spell your last name for us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. McCloskey, my name is Milomir Obrenovic, Dragan. Obrenovic, Dragan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. McCloskey, wait a minute. I think that the witness has to make a solemn declaration. Good afternoon, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I understand, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may sit down, please. Yes, Mr. McCloskey. You may proceed. Examined by Mr. McCloskey:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Obrenovic, have you had a chance to carefully look at the indictment against you in this case?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have had an occasion to do so, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And after reviewing that indictment and consulting with your counsel and entering a plea agreement with the Office of the Prosecutor, did you plead guilty to that indictment?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did plead guilty.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: I'm going to have to object because that's a misstatement of his plea. He pled guilty to one count in the indictment, prosecutions, not to the whole indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Well, for clarification purposes. The public is not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, if you want to be more specific, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you plead guilty to the persecutions count of that indictment which included all the facts of the indictment?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you stand by that plea today?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in your plea agreement, you agreed to testify truthfully as a Prosecution witness. Do you stand by that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that plea agreement and materials is P115, Your Honours. Mr. Obrenovic, can you tell us where you were born.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC
utterances.text: I was born in Rogatica, the Rogatica Municipality in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC
utterances.text: On the 12th of April, 1963.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where is Rogatica in relation to, let's say, Srebrenica roughly?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, Rogatica in relation to Srebrenica is situated to the southwest, on the road from Sarajevo to Gorazde. It is in Eastern Bosnia, in fact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Roughly about how far away from the Srebrenica area?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC
utterances.text: Taking the road, about 150 kilometres. As the crow flies, it's nearer, of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where did you grow up?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC
utterances.text: I grew up in Rogatica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where did you go to school?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC
utterances.text: I went to primary school in Rogatica, and to secondary school in Belgrade, the military gymnasium there. Then I went to the military academy for the ground forces. I graduated after two years in Belgrade and spent a further two years in Banja Luka. And that was my schooling.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe how old were you when you first began formal military training?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know what you consider by "formal military training." I went to military school at the age of 15, and I received a commission.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Well let's talk about the military school --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC
utterances.text: -- As second lieutenant.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- At 15. How old were you when you graduated from that school with a commission?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I graduated from secondary school when I was 18, and the academy when I was 23 years old.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us about the -- just some about the military academy, what kind of training you received.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC
utterances.text: At the time, the military academy for the ground forces was organised in the following way: The first two years were general streams, general courses if I can put it that way. And year 3 and 4 were specialist training courses. So during the first two years, we would study general subjects and basic military training, whereas in years 3 and 4, we would undertake specialist courses for the branches and services. I was in the armoured and mechanised units sector, so I was trained within that sphere, for armoured and mechanised units.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What year did you graduate?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC
utterances.text: I graduated in 1986.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As a second lieutenant?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC
utterances.text: I received the rank of second lieutenant, yes, after graduation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sinatra.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but Mr. McCloskey is leading the witness. But for foundation purposes, I'm going to ask the Court just to recognise that I'll allow him to lead the witness for foundation purposes at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Upon graduation as a second lieutenant, what assignment did you receive? What did you do after graduation?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC
utterances.text: I went further on to do professional military service in the Jastrebarsko garrison in the Republic of Croatia. And I was the commander for the tank platoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how long were you in that job as the commander of the tank platoon?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC
utterances.text: I was a commander or komandir of the tank platoon for six months.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then what was your job?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC
utterances.text: After that, I took up the post of commander of the tank company.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was that in the same location, or were you transferred somewhere?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was in the same garrison, the Jastrebarsko garrison, the same brigade, in fact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And can you now just briefly go through your military career describing your various assignments, what years you had them, up until the beginning of the war in Bosnia in 1992.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC
utterances.text: So I was commander of the tank company until 1990. In 1990, I started being acting deputy commander of the armoured battalion. And I remained in that position until I came to Bosnia. When the war started in Croatia and when the Yugoslav People's Army started withdrawing from Croatia, the unit that I was serving in was relocated to Tuzla, the Dubrave airport. We came there, the entire unit, in the month of October 1991, and that is when I became acting commander of the armoured battalion. Then I became acting commander. Before that, I was acting deputy commander. On the 28th of February, 1992, this battalion was entrusted with the task of being relocated to Mali Zvornik and Zvornik, and that's where we happened to be when the war broke out in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what was your position when you were stationed in Mali Zvornik at the time the war broke out?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC
utterances.text: I had the duty of the commander of the armoured battalion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you just continue describing your career as -- after the war broke out.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC
utterances.text: This unit and I, along with it, remained in the mentioned site, at the Mali Zvornik and Zvornik locations until the Yugoslav People's Army withdrew from Bosnia-Herzegovina. That is to say, the 19th of May, 1992. This unit was relocated to the Vrsac garrison on the 20th of May, 1992. And I went with that unit to the Vrsac garrison. I stayed there all the way up to the 1st of December, 1992. But I was returned for Zvornik for a period of 30 days. To be more precise, between the 15th of June, 1992, until the 20th of July the same year, I was sent there to help out. I spent the rest of the time, as I already said, at the Vrsac garrison. On the 1st of December, 1992, I was given orders to go to the Army of Republika Srpska. I reported at Crna Rijeka and I was stationed in the Drina Corps. And from there, I was appointed acting chief of staff of the 1st Zvornik Infantry Brigade. And that's where I practically spent most of the time during the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how long were you the chief of staff of the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC
utterances.text: I was appointed as acting chief of staff first. That was on the 1st of December, 1992, somewhere up to the month of April 1993. And that is when I was appointed chief of staff actually. I was chief of staff practically all the way up to when everything that happened in Srebrenica started. From the 4th of July, 1995, I was deputy commander of the Zvornik Brigade until the 15th of July, until about noon, when I continued performing my duties as chief of staff in accordance with the establishment. On the 8th of August, 1995, I was appointed acting commander of the Zvornik infantry brigade, and I remained in that position until the 15th of September the same year. After that, again, I was chief of staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you just continue through the period of your arrest.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC
utterances.text: Then I was chief of staff all the way up to the 30th of April, 1996, when I was appointed acting commander of the 303rd Motorised Brigade, as it was known by then. And I was in this position then, deputy commander of the 303rd Motorised Brigade until, I think, August 1998 when I was appointed commander of the 505th, because by then the 303rd had been turned into the 505th. And I remained in that position until my arrest on the 15th of May, 2001 -- no, I'm sorry. It was the 15th of April. 15th of April, 2001.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So was the 303rd and the 505th formerly known as the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe for the Court the duties of a chief of staff, just try to give them a broad outline to give them a feel for what your job was, what your duties and responsibilities were throughout the wartime period up until you became actually commander of the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC
utterances.text: I'll try. The duties of a chief of staff are rather complex. According to the establishment, the chief of staff is at the same time the deputy commander of the brigade. He is practically the head of the staff in the brigade. He controls the staff of the brigade and practically it is planning that is within his ambit to put it as briefly as possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court what the staff is made up of, what officers, what units?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, the staff is part of the command of the brigade. Now I am specifically speaking about the staff of the brigade, the staff is part of the command of the brigade. And specifically, I'm going to be talking about the Zvornik Brigade at that time. So it was headed by a chief of staff. And then there was the operations and teaching section which was headed by the assistant chief of staff for teaching and operations affairs. And then he had three or four officers in this regard. Then the next section was the section for personnel affairs, and this assistant commander also had two officers, one for the replenishment of manpower, the other one for personnel. And then there was the assistant commander of the section for intelligence and security. Then there was the organ of the arms and services. According to the establishment of the Zvornik Brigade, it was the head of engineering who was there. Then there was the head of communications signals. We had a chief of signals. We were supposed to have an head of anti-aircraft defence, but we didn't have one. Then we were supposed to have a chief for artillery, but we didn't have one either. And then also one for BHO. We did have one of those. In addition to that, the staff had a staff office involving two persons. One person took care of the mail, and the rest -- or rather, this other person was practically involved in typing and other such matters. And then there was the command of the actual -- there was the staff officer. So that is all as far as I can recall right now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So all those positions you mentioned were part of a staff that you oversaw?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, in the translation I got, it said that you were -- you oversaw the intelligence and security units. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC
utterances.text: No, it is not correct. Only the intelligence section, only intelligence. There were two sections in the command. There was security, directly subordinated to the commander, and the other one was for intelligence affairs, and that was within the staff. These are two different entities involving different people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So who was the security officer for the Zvornik Brigade that was directly under the commander?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC
utterances.text: At the time of what happened in Srebrenica, the assistant for security was Second Lieutenant Drago Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you briefly describe for the Court, you've described the staff. What other officers served the commander in the organisation besides yourself, the staff, the security officer? What other assistant commanders were there?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC
utterances.text: If you allow me, in order to present this picturesquely, the commander of the brigade has three entities. One entity has the staff of the brigade. Perhaps I can put that first. Then the second entity is logistics, the entire group that has to do with logistics. And the third entity are assistant commanders, or rather, the section for morale, the section for security. So assistant commanders were the following persons: The assistant commander for security. At that time, it was Second Lieutenant Drago Nikolic. Then there was assistant commander for morale, religious and legal affairs, and the assistant commander for logistics.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you just briefly describe what the assistant commander for morale, religious, and legal affairs did?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC
utterances.text: He was head of that section that we referred to just now, the assistant commander for morale, religious, and legal affairs. To put it very briefly and in the simplest possible terms, there were a few people in this section who were involved in matters related to combat morale, information issues, practical issues that involved burials, visits to wounded men, information, things that belonged to that section.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who was that assistant commander in July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC
utterances.text: In the Zvornik Brigade in July 1995, the assistant commander for morale was Major Nenad Simic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was the assistant commander for logistics in the Zvornik Brigade at that time?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC
utterances.text: The assistant commander for logistics of the Zvornik Brigade at the time was Captain Sretan Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe for us in more detail what the logistics organ did. What was their -- what were their main tasks?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC
utterances.text: With your permission, I would portray this properly if I were to refer to all the organs involved in their service. So in the section for logistics of the Zvornik Brigade was the traffic service, the technical service, the medical service, and the financial service. And there was also veterinarian. And the names themselves show what they dealt with. So the traffic service planned traffic and provided security for them, practically for the units of the brigade. The technical service ensured the technical aspect of the life of the units. That is to say, maintenance and repair of vehicles and ammunition systems and ammunition and things that had to do with fuel. So in the roughest possible terms, that is what was done by way of overhaul. Then the quartermasters provided uniforms, clothing, et cetera. Then the medical corps took care of the medical aspect, that is to say treating the wounded and so on and so forth. And the veterinarian service also examined animals that were later used for food and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Along with the staff and the assistant commanders in the departments you described, were there actual infantry battalions in the Zvornik Brigade at the time?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In addition to the command that we spoke of just now, the Zvornik Brigade had units within it that were battalions, divisions, companies, and one independent platoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many infantry battalions did Zvornik have in July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC
utterances.text: In July 1995, the Zvornik Brigade had seven infantry battalions, and they were numbered from 1 to 7.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you give me roughly how many men were in a battalion.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC
utterances.text: In these mentioned seven infantry battalions, the average numbers involved from 450 up to 550 men. It changed from month to month.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. What other units were in the Zvornik Brigade besides the infantry battalions?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC
utterances.text: Besides the infantry battalions, we had a manoeuvre battalion that was called the Wolves from the Drina, Vukovica Drina or the Podrinjski Odred, or detachment depending on the papers that we see. There were also divisions. One division for artillery and another one for anti-aircraft support. There were a few companies, including the signals company, the engineering company, the military police company. Then the mentioned staff officers, and there was the logistics battalion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many military policemen were in the military police company?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC
utterances.text: Again, in different periods it varied. If I remember correctly, there were between 95 to 110 of them depending on the period involved. But that was the range.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the engineering company, how many men were in the engineering company?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC
utterances.text: If I remember correctly, they had between 80 to 100 soldiers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who was the commander of the engineering company in July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC
utterances.text: In July of 1995, the commander of the engineering company was Dragan Jevtic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And going back to your staff that you described, one of the staff positions you described, I believe, is chief of engineers. Who was the chief of engineer in July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC
utterances.text: In July 1995, the chief of engineer was Major Dragan Jokic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you see Mr. Jokic in Court today?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is he sitting with his hand on his chin next to the security guard?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry, that's not an independent identification of the accused when he describes him as he's sitting there with his hand. I would like an independent identification by Mr. Obrenovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, yes, you're right at this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I wasn't aware identification was an issue, Your Honour. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, normally it's not a big issue in this courtroom, but when you ask the witness to identify somebody, you give a very obvious indication.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I did that on purpose obviously because I didn't think it was an issue. I'm sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you see Dragan Jokic in the courtroom today?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC
utterances.text: I do see him, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe for us where he is.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC
utterances.text: On my left, the fourth person in this row where I sit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let the record reflect that he has identified Mr. Jokic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. McCloskey, he said "the fourth person in this row where I sit." What does it mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This is why I tried to cheat earlier, Your Honour. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you try to do a little -- I've got a better angle than the Judges do on the rows. So if you could try to do a little better, a little clearer explanation of where Mr. Jokic is, we can sort that out.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC
utterances.text: To the left of the guard. This is the door that I walked through. The first person sitting there is the guard, and the next person is Mr. Jokic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, can you describe for us what the activities of -- the normal activities of the engineering company were throughout the war.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC
utterances.text: They worked in different periods of time, but this is primarily what they did. From the domain of engineering, that is to say laying mines, establishing minefields in the advance area and in other areas, and also the maintenance of minefields. Then also the building of fortifications. These are dugouts for ammunition and for soldiers. Then building roads, communication roads and so on. Generally speaking, work from that domain.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did the engineering company in the period of around July 1995 have any heavy equipment?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you just describe to us - I don't need precise detail, but what you recall - what kind of heavy equipment they had.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC
utterances.text: In July 1995?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC
utterances.text: In July 1995 in the engineering company, there was part of this equipment that we had from the military fund. That is to say what was owned by the Army of Republika Srpska. And when necessary, certain machinery could have been mobilised when it was needed. For the most part, we used this heavy mechanisation by way of various bulldozers, the ones we had there at the time. They were either owned by us or by companies that made them available to us. And then various digging machinery, loaders, and then trucks for transporting different kinds of cargo, a few tractors. That's about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And the -- where was the location of the brigade command? The brigade command headquarters? Just roughly. We'll get a map later on to get more precise.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC
utterances.text: The command and the staff of the Zvornik Brigade were at the Standard barracks. This is the former footwear factory Standard in Karakaj. I think this was about 3 kilometres downstream, or to the north of the town of Zvornik, right on the banks of the Drina River.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did the engineering company have its own building or headquarters?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC
utterances.text: The engineering company was stationed in another building that our brigade had, also in Karakaj. But further to the north on the road towards Bijeljina, perhaps a kilometre away from the brigade command. That's where there were some prefabricated buildings of the youth centre, and that is where that company was staying.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What else in the way of equipment or buildings were at the engineering company headquarters?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC
utterances.text: It was five or six prefabricated buildings if I can remember correctly. That's where the soldiers slept. Officers were nearby. Also there were weapons and masks, protection masks and other related equipment. Whatever a unit of that format would have. And then there were some mining devices, ammunition and storage. Perhaps some spare parts for the maintenance of technical equipment, for signals equipment, some food. That would be about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were the excavators and loaders you talked about? Where were those normally kept when they weren't working?

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: I'm sorry the witness has not mentioned excavators or loaders. That was not mentioned in this testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I think the correct word is bulldozers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I thought he mentioned all three, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, you may ask a question to this witness what kind of equipment. When we have this confirmed, you may proceed with this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us what kind of heavy equipment the engineering company had in July -- around July of 1995.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, the engineers company in the period we're discussing had heavy machinery of the following type: First, various types of trucks, dump trucks, for the transport of various loads, cargos. Then the other machinery was as follows: It had diggers, one or two of those. I don't remember the types. Then bulldozers, also two or three types. And ULTs. So those were the machines that were used. Now, property-wise, some of them belonged to us. That is to say, the Army of Republika Srpska. They were the owners of the machinery. And the other portion of the machinery was requisitioned from firms in Zvornik that had that kind of machinery.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, did you say that we have a rovokopac?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I said kopac, diggers. I don't know whether that's the right term. I'm not an engineers' man myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sinatra.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, but Mr. McCloskey is leading the witness. He never said -- I'm sorry I can't pronounce. Mr. McCloskey put that term in his testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think she is wrong, Your Honour. We had this problem, I think, before with the translations of the various things. It really isn't an issue in contention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sinatra.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, the witness himself said he didn't say that word.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, maybe the witness will be the right person for this question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Obrenovic, can you describe the duties of the chief of engineering and how he related to the engineering company. But first, you could describe the duties and responsibilities of the chief of engineers, Mr. Jokic, in 1995.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC
utterances.text: As I've already said, Mr. Jokic was chief of the engineers within the various arms in the brigade headquarters. And roughly speaking, the duties of the chief of engineers would be as follows: First, we have planning. It would be his duty to plan and propose to the chief of staff or commander the deployment of engineering machines and machinery in combat or for combat. He would also propose in the process of decision-making, decisions with respect to securing the engineers and the deployment of machinery. He would also be in charge of seeing that all the machinery is used properly once a decision has been taken to deploy it. He would also see that the soldiers in the engineering company were trained properly. And that, for the most part, would be the focus of his duties.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if one of his proposals on the use of the machinery was adopted by yourself as chief of staff or the commander, what were his responsibilities relating to the carrying out of your orders or the orders of the commander relating to engineering, the engineering job?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC
utterances.text: There were two possibilities, and the commander would decide which. In the Zvornik Brigade at that time, the commander of the engineers brigade was Jevtic Dragan, Jevtic Dragan who wasn't a professional soldier, but a reservist. Then the commander's decision was that the chief of the engineers, and not only the chief of the engineers, but also chief of communications, artillery and so on, would spend practically all his time with the unit, and then sees that his proposals are put into practice. He would assist the commander of the engineers company to carry out the orders given by the commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say that he sees to it that the -- to carry out the orders, does he have authority to issue instructions consistent with those orders?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he does, within the scope of what the commander or chief of staff ordered in the first place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you give us an example of how that might practically work, if you can recall a situation where Mr. Jokic proposed something and then assisted in having that job carried out by issuing instructions.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC
utterances.text: Well, for example, the most common situation was when we were building a road between one and another battalion, for example. And the chief of the engineers unit would say how this could best be done. Now, if the commander or I myself were to accept the decision he had taken and his proposal, that is, when the commander made his decision, that decision would be translated into an order, both oral -- rather, oral or written. It didn't matter. And Jokic, or rather, the chief of the engineers would put this into practice with the engineers company. There was the company commander there, but as I said, he was a reservist, so Jokic for all intents and purposes would help in putting this into practice, implementing what was ordered.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So was Mr. Jokic a reservist?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC
utterances.text: No, no. The commander of the engineers company was the reservist. He was a reserve soldier acting as a commander. Komandir Jokic was a professional soldier like myself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you briefly describe what knowledge you have regarding Mr. Jokic's military training and experience, just briefly.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, I really can't give you any details. I can tell you roughly that Major Jokic graduated from military academy in the engineers, and that in the JNA he always served in the engineers units. I know that he is a qualified engineers man. Now, as to the details, I really can't say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Can you describe for the Court the duties and responsibilities of the brigade operations duty officer.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC
utterances.text: You mean the duty officer? The duties of a duty officer can be general and specific. The general duties are prescribed by the rules of services in the army, and they are the same for all operations, duty offices in the brigades of the army. And these would be as follows, roughly speaking: They must be well acquainted with the situation, the tasks, and deployment of his subordinate units, the battalions, companies, et cetera, of the Zvornik Brigade. He must also monitor the situation in the area of responsibility of his unit in the brigade, the duty officer which he is. Next, to monitor the situation in neighbouring -- in his neighbouring units, that is to say, brigades on his left and to his right. Next, to monitor the situation on the adjoining territory and maintain links with the subordinate units with battalions and companies. And to maintain links and communication with the centre of civil defence in Zvornik as well as communications with the MUP, and communications with his superior, or rather duty operative commands of the Drina Corps. Next, he would have to have an overview of the units that are deployed outside the area of the Zvornik Brigade, in the different terrains in the field, and monitor units who are on special assignment and on various states -- in states of emergency and on various states of alert. Next, following orders by the brigade commander or the duty officer in the Drina Corps, he can issue orders to subordinate duty officers in battalions and independent companies. Next, another of his duties would be in extraordinary situations and extraordinary times, to issue orders to subordinate duty officers. And as soon as possible, to report back to the brigade commander and the duty office in the Drina Corps of the latest developments. That for the most part to the best of my recollections would be most of the general duties that a brigade operations duty officer would have. Now, special duties in the brigade, in the shortest possible terms would be as follows: They would be regulated by the corps commander and would involve a list of duty officers when the shifts take place, what type of uniforms are to be worn during shiftwork, the logbooks and records kept of shifts. So practical, technical details. So these special duties were specific to each unit, and the Zvornik Brigade had its general tasks and then the units would have their specific tasks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how long did a duty officer's shift normally last?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC
utterances.text: The rules of service provided for 24-hour shifts, and that's what it was like. Due to certain circumstances, shifts would be longer or shorter, but this was pursuant to decisions taken by a commander under extraordinary circumstances.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there a normal starting time for this 24-hour shift?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC
utterances.text: If I remember correctly, that would be around 8.00 or 9.00 in the morning. The shifts would replace each other I think at 8.00 a.m.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how was it determined who would be holding the duty officer position for a 24-hour period?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC
utterances.text: The commander would prescribe a list and the order of duty operations officers. And then he would list the officers. Higher ranking officers were duty officers, and there were assistants, too. Then one of the staff from the operations department on the list -- on the basis of this list of duty officers would compile another list for each individual day. The lists would be compiled for a fortnight in advance, and it would be adjusted if the need arose because two weeks was a rather long period of time for planning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So if we have a duty officer and an assistant -- first, let me ask you, from whom did the commander allow duty officer positions to be filled by? What people were qualified by your commander to be in the duty officer position?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC
utterances.text: At the time, the duty officers would be everybody except the commander and myself. So the assistant commanders, the various chiefs of the different arms and services, and the departments and sectors mentioned. But they would be commanding officers with higher ranks which knew the position and situation in the brigade, at least roughly, based on their experience.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How about Drago Nikolic, the chief of security? Did he have to do his tour of the duty officer job?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he would be a duty officer, too, although there was some conflict between him and the commander. But yes, he was a duty officer, too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe the conflict you mean. What are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC
utterances.text: Drago Nikolic, as a security officer, asked to be relieved of working as a duty officer because of the responsibilities he had in this other area. However, the commander did not accept that; and as a result, there was a certain amount of -- well, not conflict. I might have used the wrong word. But friction, let's say. There was a certain amount of friction.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Was Mr. Jokic, Dragan Jokic, ever a duty officer?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was on the list of duty officers. And he would take up his duties according to the list. When his name was down for it and when he didn't have any other jobs to do in the field elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How about the assistant duty officers? What sorts of people were allowed to hold that post?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC
utterances.text: The assistants were mostly people with lower ranks and lower positions. Officers with lower ranks or NCOs, that kind of thing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was the job of the assistant duty officer?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC
utterances.text: The duty officer would be up for a break at 1.00 a.m., and he was required to be ready for duty by 6.00 a.m. So after midnight, his assistant would replace him and deal with any urgent matters. During the day, he would be at hand to help the duty officer and go about the regular business of a duty officer's assistant; that is to say, he would be in charge of the cashbox, documents, things like that. He would see that everything was stored properly and that everything was in order.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did the duty officer work?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC
utterances.text: There was an office at the headquarters in the building of the brigade headquarters, and that was called the office of the duty officer. The office had a table, some communications devices which allowed him to maintain communications with the persons I listed earlier on. He would have maps with the areas in which the units were deployed, and that's where he would spend his time on duty.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What floor was that on, the duty officer room?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC
utterances.text: In the headquarters, it would be on the first floor, the upper storey, the first room by the staircase on the landing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where was that in relation to the -- to your office, the chief of staff?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC
utterances.text: The chief of staff's office was on the same floor. You went down the corridor to the very end, and it would be the one but last office on the right-hand side. That's where my office was, or the chief of staff's.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where was the commander's office in relation to your office and the duty officer's office?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC
utterances.text: The commander's office was opposite my office.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the other side of a hallway? Is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. Mine was to the right; his was to the left of the corridor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned communications equipment in the duty office. Can you describe as best as you can recall what kind of equipment.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC
utterances.text: If I remember correctly, there were telephones, and it would be linked to a switchboard within the barracks, an internal line. Then there was another telephone with a wire communication with all the battalion commands. That's two telephones. There was a third telephone which was an ordinary civilian telephone. 076 was the code. And another extension which was connected to the switchboard.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where was the switchboard?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC
utterances.text: The switchboard was on the upper storey in the same headquarters building, to the left. When you went a floor higher, it would be on the left to the right of the corridor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If the duty officer wished to call and speak to someone at the Drina Corps in Vlasenica, how would they do it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC
utterances.text: He could do so in the following way: First of all, he could use the civilian telephone, just like any other civilian, an ordinary civilian telephone. The next possibility would be to use a radio relay device, RAT, with the help of the switchboard. So he would have to ring up the switchboard, ask for Zlatar, and then through this radio relay device, they would be able to connect him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you confirm to us what Zlatar is.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC
utterances.text: Zlatar was the code name for the command of the Drina Corps in the plan for the communications.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the way you just described going to the Drina Corps command or Zlatar through the switchboard, could that be a protected, safe line, or was that an open line?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC
utterances.text: It was I would say an open line, because it was an radio relay R800 device which would be listened into.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. How about the civilian line? How secure was that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the civilian line could be tapped. But it appeared later on that it was less tapped into than the other relay line and turned out to be safer, in fact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the civilian line an actual wire line?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC
utterances.text: It was both a wire line across the floor, and it was also a link.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "link," what do you mean?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC
utterances.text: Well, a relay device once again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "tapped into," what do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC
utterances.text: The radio relay device used radio relay waves to put out modulated sound signals.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So have you described all the ways a duty officer can communicate now?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC
utterances.text: The command of the Drina Corps, there was another possibility. And that was through the use of a code station, an encrypted teleprinter device. But this implied the transference of written information, and that was completely secure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there...

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'll get it out. I'm sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there a relay centre somewhere above Standard that assisted in these communications?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC
utterances.text: There was a communications centre on a hill above Zvornik, and that was able to establish radio communication which could also be intercepted. The other thing that existed was the radio relay interim centre. That could also be intercepted. Then there was the civilian telephone, as I've already said, and the coded, encrypted station which coded written messages, and that was a secure line which could not be intercepted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where was this radio centre you just described?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC
utterances.text: The radio relay intermediary centre -- or interim centre was at Gucevo which was a hill on the way to Loznica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the duty operations officer have a radio that he could communicate on as opposed to the telephones and the lines and the switchboard you were talking about?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC
utterances.text: He would use one of those telephones, that is to say, they would connect him at the switchboard. So yes, he could. He could have a radio communication. Not directly, but through the switchboard at the radio centre.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you explain - maybe this should be the last question - how that switchboard -- what that switchboard could connect the duty officer to.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC
utterances.text: The switchboard could connect the duty officer to all subordinate units, all the battalions, divisions, and companies that we mentioned earlier on, whether inside the barracks or deployed at their positions somewhere. Next, it could ensure communication with the superior command, or rather the command of the Drina Corps, the Drina Corps headquarters. And via that, with the main staff, and with neighbouring units as well, the Bratunac Brigade, for example, the 1st Birac Brigade, and the other units which were Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Obrenovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, it's time...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Well, Mr. Obrenovic, now you are a witness in this case, and you are under the oath. So during the period you're under the oath, do not talk to anybody about your testimony, and do not let anybody talk to you about it. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, I have understood.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I will not remind you every time. I just remind you once. You have to remember it until you have finished your testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We'll resume at 9.00 tomorrow morning. The hearing is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
